chapters.title: Physics and Mathematics
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces the mathematical framework essential for studying physics, including vectors and scalars, vector algebra, differential calculus, and integral calculus. It also covers errors in measurement and the concept of significant digits. The chapter establishes the mathematical language that underpins all subsequent physical analysis.

events.text: Vectors add by triangle rule, not ordinary addition
Resultant = 5 m/s at 53° from intended path
Equal vectors: same magnitude + same direction
Two vectors are equal ONLY IF: same magnitude AND same direction
Parallel translation leaves a vector unchanged
Same tail → complete parallelogram → diagonal = sum
Equal vectors → resultant = 2A cos(θ/2), bisects angle
Subtract vectors: flip, then add. New angle → new magnitude.
Subtraction = flip + add. Angle changes; formula stays the same.
Positive scalar → same direction, magnitude multiplied
Vector a from origin O at angle alpha to X-axis
x-component = a cos alpha, y-component = a cos beta
Component along direction = a cos(angle with that direction)
Rope force = 20 N at 60° above horizontal
Resolution: a = a cos(alpha) i-hat + a cos(beta) j-hat
dot product measures 'alignment' of two vectors
angle theta between the two vectors
Result is a scalar — just a number, not a vector
Perpendicular force → zero work, zero energy transfer

events.text: Area under curve = region between curve, x-axis, and two vertical lines
Definite integral = exact area under curve (infinite thin bars)
Sum of AP: S = (N/2)(first + last) = (N/2)(a + b − Δx)
Antiderivative of x → ½x², d/dx(½x²) = x ✓

events.text: To evaluate: antiderivative → plug in limits → subtract
Least count = smallest subdivision on scale
Significant digits = certain digits + one doubtful digit
Use scientific notation to remove ambiguity

events.title: Zeros After the Decimal — Two Rules

events.text: 14.750 → next digit is 5, 7 is odd → round up → 14.8
14.650 × 10^12 → next digit is 5, 6 is even → leave unchanged → 14.6 × 10^12
Add/subtract → drop digits right of first doubtful column
4.2 km ÷ 0.25 h → 2 sig. dig. vs 2 sig. dig. → answer: 17 km/h
Random errors can't be removed — average many results to approach the true value
True value lies within x-bar ± sigma

OA=OB=OC=R; OA & OC symmetric about OB

chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_1>>
If I told you a car is moving at sixty kilometers per hour, would you know everything about its motion? What if it's heading straight toward a wall? Speed alone isn't the whole story — direction matters too. <<SECTION:Scalars vs Vectors|id=sec-1>> Some quantities are perfectly described by just a number and a unit. <<WRITE_TEXT:Scalar = number + unit only|id=text-1>> Mass is the classic example. Five kilograms plus two kilograms simply equals seven kilograms — ordinary addition, nothing surprising. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:arrow-5ms>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_1:diagram_vector_arrow>> But velocity refuses to behave that simply. <<WRITE_TEXT:Vector = magnitude + direction|id=text-2>> Saying 'five meters per second' tells you how fast, but not where. A vector needs both pieces of information to be complete, and we draw it as an arrow — the length shows the size, and the arrow shows the direction. <<TRACE:arrow-5ms>> <<PAUSE:short>> The back end of the arrow is called the tail, and the pointy front end is called the head. <<WRITE_TEXT:Tail = start, Head = arrowhead|id=text-3>> Different directions, different arrows — even if the speed is the same number. <<POINT:arrow-tail-label>> <<POINT:arrow-tail-label>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Now here's the interesting question: <<SECTION:Adding Vectors|id=sec-2>> what happens when a particle has TWO velocities acting on it at the same time — in completely different directions? Can you just add the numbers? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:ball-velocity-arrow>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_1:diagram_ball_tube>> Let's find out. A small ball is moving inside a long tube at a speed of three meters per second along the tube. At the same time, the tube itself is sliding sideways in the room at four meters per second — perpendicular to the tube's own length. <<TRACE:ball-velocity-arrow>> <<FOCUS:tube-velocity-arrow>> After one second, the ball has moved three meters in the direction along the tube, and four meters sideways — because the tube dragged it. <<WRITE_STEP:Ball moves 3 m along tube|id=step-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Tube moves 4 m sideways|id=step-2>> Those two displacements are at right angles to each other. <<TRACE:tube-velocity-arrow>> <<FOCUS:triangle-outline>> Draw both of those as sides of a right-angled triangle, and the actual path the ball took — the resultant — is the diagonal, the hypotenuse. <<WRITE_STEP:Resultant² = 3² + 4²|id=step-3>> Three squared plus four squared equals nine plus sixteen, which is twenty-five. So the resultant displacement is five meters. <<TRACE:triangle-outline>> The resultant is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle — so we use the Pythagorean theorem: square both speeds, add them, and take the square root. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v_{\text{resultant}} = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9+16} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \text{ m/s}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:resultant-arrow>> And the direction? Simple geometry gives us an angle of fifty-three degrees from the tube direction. <<WRITE_STEP:Direction = 53° from tube|id=step-4>> So the resultant velocity of the ball is five meters per second at fifty-three degrees from the tube. <<WRITE_ANSWER:5 m/s at 53° from tube|id=ans-1>> <<POINT:resultant-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> Notice: three plus four is seven, but the real answer is five — not seven! You cannot just add vector magnitudes as if they were scalars. The direction is part of the calculation. That is the whole point of vectors. <<WRITE_KEY:Vectors add by triangle rule, not ordinary addition|id=key-1>> <<POINT:triangle-outline>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Extended Example — Swimmer|id=sec-3>> Here's one more. Imagine a swimmer crossing a river. She swims straight across at three meters per second, but the river current pushes her downstream at four meters per second — exactly perpendicular to her swimming direction. What is her actual speed across the water? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Same triangle rule: three meters per second and four meters per second at right angles. <<WRITE_STEP:Speed² = 3² + 4² = 25|id=step-5>> The resultant speed is five meters per second, and she ends up moving at fifty-three degrees from her intended direction. She arrives downstream — not straight across. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Resultant = 5 m/s at 53° from intended path|id=ans-2>> That's the power of knowing vectors: the answer is five, not seven. So the big idea to carry with you: scalars are fully described by a number and a unit alone — mass, temperature, time. Vectors need both magnitude and direction — velocity, force, displacement. And when vectors combine, you use the triangle rule, not ordinary arithmetic. <<WRITE_KEY:Scalar: number+unit. Vector: magnitude+direction.|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_2>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Imagine two arrows — both exactly five centimetres long. Are they equal? Not necessarily. Because a vector isn't just a size — it's a size AND a direction. Miss either one, and you have a completely different vector. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_2:equality_diagram>> <<SECTION:What makes two vectors equal?|id=sec-1>>Let's put two vectors side by side and ask the question properly. Here are two arrows — same length, same direction — just drawn in different spots on the page. <<TRACE:vec-a1>> <<TRACE:vec-a1>> <<FOCUS:equal-label>> <<FOCUS:equal-label>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Equal vectors: same magnitude + same direction|id=text-1>>Notice — they don't need to start at the same point. Their position on the page is irrelevant. What matters is that they point the same way and stretch the same distance. Those two vectors ARE equal. <<POINT:equal-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:vec-b1>> Now look at this second pair. Same length again — but one points right and the other points straight up. <<TRACE:vec-b1>> <<WRITE_KEY:Two vectors are equal ONLY IF: same magnitude AND same direction|id=key-1>>So here is the question — are these two equal? <<POINT:vec-b2>> <<POINT:vec-b2>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:unequal-label>> No — they are NOT equal. The magnitudes match, but the directions are completely different. Both conditions must hold — magnitude AND direction. One out of two is not enough. <<POINT:unequal-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> Think about two cars, both moving at sixty kilometres per hour. One heads north, the other heads east. Their speed is the same — but their velocity vectors are completely different, because direction is part of the vector. <<FOCUS:vec-a1>> Now here is something elegant. Look back at our equal pair. What if I pick up one of those arrows and slide it across the page — keeping it perfectly parallel to itself, never rotating it? <<TRACE:vec-a1>> <<FOCUS:vec-a2>> It is still the same vector. Sliding a vector — a parallel translation — changes nothing about it. The magnitude hasn't changed. The direction hasn't changed. The vector is identical. <<POINT:vec-a2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Parallel translation leaves a vector unchanged|id=text-2>>This is why in physics we are free to move vectors around when we add them or analyse them — as long as we never tilt them. Position is NOT part of what defines a vector. <<POINT:vec-a2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:equal-label>> So the rule is clean and absolute: two vectors are equal if and only if both their magnitude and their direction are the same. Change one, you change the vector. Slide it freely — you change nothing. <<POINT:equal-label>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_3>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> If you walk three steps east and then four steps north, have you actually walked seven steps? Your legs say no — so why does normal addition lie to you here? The answer is that directions matter. When quantities have both size AND direction, we need a smarter kind of addition. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_3:triangle_parallelogram>> <<SECTION:Triangle Rule|id=sec-1>>Here is the key idea. <<WRITE_TEXT:Tip-to-tail: resultant goes start → finish|id=text-1>>To add vector a and vector b, draw a first, then place the tail of b right at the head of a — like two arrows chained together. <<TRACE:vector-a>> <<TRACE:vector-a>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:resultant-triangle>> The resultant — the sum — is the single arrow that goes from the very tail of a all the way to the very tip of b. It is the shortcut that replaces both journeys. <<TRACE:resultant-triangle>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:vector-a-parallel>> <<SECTION:Parallelogram Rule|id=sec-2>>There is a second, equivalent way: draw both vectors starting from the SAME point. <<WRITE_TEXT:Same tail → complete parallelogram → diagonal = sum|id=text-2>>They become two sides of a parallelogram. The diagonal through the shared tail is the very same resultant. <<TRACE:vector-a-parallel>> <<TRACE:vector-a-parallel>> <<FOCUS:diagonal-resultant>> Complete the dashed sides and the diagonal emerges — same direction, same length as before. Two rules, one truth. <<TRACE:diagonal-resultant>> <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_3:magnitude_direction>> <<SECTION:Magnitude & Direction|id=sec-3>>But how LONG is this resultant, and which way does it point? Let the angle between a and b be theta. <<WRITE_TEXT:Angle between vectors = θ|id=text-3>>I drop a perpendicular from the far corner of the parallelogram down to the baseline. That creates a right triangle hiding inside the diagram. <<TRACE:angle-theta>> <<PAUSE:long>> The magnitude of the resultant is found from the big right triangle inside the parallelogram — it's the square root of a squared plus b squared plus two a b cosine theta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:|\vec{a}+\vec{b}| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + 2ab\cos\theta}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:perpendicular-DE>> The base of that right triangle is a plus b cosine theta, and the height is b sine theta. <<WRITE_STEP:AD² = (a + b cosθ)² + (b sinθ)²|id=step-1>>So by the Pythagorean theorem, the diagonal squared equals the base squared plus the height squared — which expands to a squared plus b squared plus two a b cosine theta. <<POINT:perpendicular-DE>> The angle alpha that the resultant makes with a equals the arctan of the opposite side over the adjacent side in that right triangle — b sine theta over a plus b cosine theta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tan\alpha = \frac{b\sin\theta}{a + b\cos\theta}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:diagonal-AD>> <<WRITE_STEP:Resultant = √(a² + b² + 2ab cosθ)|id=step-2>>So the magnitude of a plus b is the square root of a squared plus b squared plus two a b cosine theta. And the angle alpha it makes with a comes from the same right triangle: tangent of alpha equals b sine theta over a plus b cosine theta. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:side-AB>> <<SECTION:Equal-Magnitude Example|id=sec-4>>Now a beautiful special case. Both vectors have equal magnitude A, and the angle between them is theta. What is the resultant? <<WRITE_TEXT:Both magnitudes = A, angle = θ|id=text-4>>We plug into the formula: under the square root we get A squared plus A squared plus two A squared cosine theta. <<PAUSE:long>> When both magnitudes are equal to A, the formula simplifies beautifully — two A squared times one plus cosine theta, and using the double-angle identity that becomes two A cosine of theta over two. <<WRITE_EQUATION:B = \sqrt{A^2 + A^2 + 2A^2\cos\theta} = 2A\cos\frac{\theta}{2}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<WRITE_STEP:B = √(2A²(1 + cosθ))|id=step-3>>That is the square root of two A squared times one plus cosine theta. Now here is the trick: one plus cosine theta equals two cosine squared of theta over two. So the whole thing becomes the square root of four A squared cosine squared of theta over two. <<POINT:angle-theta>> Plugging equal magnitudes into the direction formula, both A's cancel and the whole expression collapses to tangent of theta over two — so alpha equals theta over two exactly. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tan\alpha = \frac{A\sin\theta}{A + A\cos\theta} = \tan\frac{\theta}{2} \implies \alpha = \frac{\theta}{2}|id=eq-4|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:diagonal-AD>> <<WRITE_STEP:B = 2A cos(θ/2)|id=step-4>>The square root of a perfect square is just itself — so the resultant magnitude is exactly two A cosine of theta over two. <<WRITE_KEY:Equal vectors → resultant = 2A cos(θ/2), bisects angle|id=key-1>>And when we check the direction formula, tangent of alpha simplifies to tangent of theta over two, giving alpha equals theta over two. <<PAUSE:short>> So when two equal vectors meet at angle theta, their resultant has magnitude two A cosine of theta over two, and it cuts the angle exactly in half — it bisects the angle between them. That is not a coincidence; the symmetry of equal magnitudes forces the result to split the middle. <<POINT:angle-alpha>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Real-World Example 1|id=sec-5>>Let's try a concrete case. A drone flies due east at five meters per second. The wind pushes it due north at five meters per second. The angle between these two velocities is ninety degrees. What is the drone's actual speed and direction? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:B = √(5² + 5² + 2×5×5×cos90°)|id=step-5>>Using our formula with a equals five, b equals five, and theta equals ninety degrees — cosine of ninety degrees is zero, so the middle term vanishes. The magnitude is the square root of twenty-five plus twenty-five, which is the square root of fifty, approximately seven point zero seven meters per second. <<WRITE_ANSWER:≈ 7.07 m/s at 45° NE|id=ans-1>>And since both components are equal, the resultant bisects the angle — pointing exactly forty-five degrees north of east. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Real-World Example 2|id=sec-6>>One more. Two tug-boats are pulling a stuck ship. Each boat pulls with a force of ten thousand newtons, and the ropes make an angle of sixty degrees with each other. What is the total force on the ship? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:B = 2×10000×cos(60°/2) = 2×10000×cos30°|id=step-6>>Equal magnitudes — so we use the clean formula: two A cosine of theta over two. That is two times ten thousand times cosine of thirty degrees. Cosine of thirty degrees is root three over two, so the resultant is ten thousand times root three, approximately seventeen thousand three hundred and twenty newtons. <<WRITE_ANSWER:≈ 17 320 N, bisecting the 60° angle|id=ans-2>>And it acts exactly along the midline between the two ropes. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<WRITE_KEY:Tip-to-tail → resultant = start to finish|id=key-2>>So the whole story of vector addition is this: chain your arrows tip to tail, and the resultant is the single arrow that closes the chain. Size and direction both matter — and the formula keeps track of both, every time. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_5>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> You already know how to add vectors — but what does it even mean to subtract one? Can you take a direction away from another direction? <<SECTION:Vector Subtraction|id=sec-1>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_5:vector_subtraction_construction>> Here's the elegant answer: subtraction is just addition in disguise. <<WRITE_TEXT:A − B = A + (−B)|id=text-1>> To subtract vector B from vector A, all you do is flip B by one hundred and eighty degrees — that gives you negative B — and then add it to A the usual tip-to-tail way. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:angle-AB>> Look at these two vectors on the board. <<WRITE_TEXT:Equal magnitudes, 60° apart|id=text-2>> Vector A and vector B both have magnitude five units, and the angle between them is sixty degrees. That angle matters — a lot. <<POINT:angle-AB>> <<POINT:angle-AB>> First, let's find A plus B — the sum. We place B tip-to-tail after A and draw the resultant. <<TRACE:resultant-sum>> <<TRACE:resultant-sum>> <<TRACE:resultant-sum>> <<FOCUS:resultant-sum>> Both vectors have magnitude five units and the angle between them is sixty degrees. <<SECTION:Part (a): Sum|id=sec-2>> Because both magnitudes are five and the angle is sixty degrees, the resultant magnitude formula gives us five times the square root of three units. Because both vectors have magnitude five and the angle between them is sixty degrees, we plug into the resultant magnitude formula and get five times root three units. <<WRITE_EQUATION:|\vec{A} + \vec{B}| = \sqrt{5^2 + 5^2 + 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 \cdot \cos 60°} = 2 \cdot 5 \cdot \cos 30° = 5\sqrt{3} \text{ units}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:A+B: angle = 60°, both magnitudes = 5|id=step-1>> Plugging in: the square root of five squared plus five squared plus two times five times five times cosine of sixty degrees simplifies to two times five times cosine of thirty degrees, which equals five root three units. <<WRITE_ANSWER:5√3 units|id=ans-1>> <<FOCUS:vector-B>> <<SECTION:Part (b): Difference|id=sec-3>> Now here's the key question: when we compute A minus B, what angle do we actually use in the formula? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:vector-neg-B>> Watch what happens when we flip B. <<WRITE_TEXT:Flip B → angle becomes 120°|id=text-3>> Vector B pointed one way — negative B points the exact opposite direction. And that flip changes the angle between A and negative B from sixty degrees to one hundred and twenty degrees. That new angle is what changes the answer. <<TRACE:vector-neg-B>> <<PAUSE:short>> Now with the angle changed to one hundred and twenty degrees, the same formula gives us a magnitude of exactly five units for the difference. <<WRITE_EQUATION:|\vec{A} - \vec{B}| = \sqrt{5^2 + 5^2 + 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 \cdot \cos 120°} = 2 \cdot 5 \cdot \cos 60° = 5 \text{ units}|id=eq-2|boxed>> The magnitude of both A and negative B is still five units — flipping a vector never changes its length, only its direction. <<WRITE_STEP:A−B: angle = 120°, both magnitudes = 5|id=step-2>> So we apply the same formula with angle one hundred and twenty degrees. <<POINT:angle-A-negB>> <<POINT:angle-A-negB>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:resultant-diff>> The square root of five squared plus five squared plus two times five times five times cosine of one hundred and twenty degrees simplifies to two times five times cosine of sixty degrees, which is exactly five units. <<WRITE_ANSWER:5 units|id=ans-2>> The sum was five root three; the difference is just five. <<TRACE:resultant-diff>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<WRITE_KEY:Subtract vectors: flip, then add. New angle → new magnitude.|id=key-1>> Let's anchor this with a real-world example. Imagine a drone flying north-east with velocity vector A, and a wind blowing due east as vector B. The relative velocity of the drone with respect to the wind is A minus B — you flip the wind vector to point west, then add it to the drone's velocity tip-to-tail. <<WRITE_TEXT:Drone: A−B = A + (−B)|id=text-4>> The angle between the drone's direction and the flipped wind vector is what you'd use in your calculation. One more scenario. A hiker walks three kilometers due east — call that vector P. Her friend walks three kilometers north-east — call that vector Q. <<SECTION:Extended Example: Hikers|id=sec-4>> The displacement of the first hiker relative to the second is P minus Q. <<WRITE_STEP:Flip Q (north-east → south-west)|id=step-3>> We flip Q — which pointed north-east — to get negative Q pointing south-west. The angle between due east and south-west is one hundred and thirty-five degrees, so the magnitude of P minus Q is the square root of three squared plus three squared plus two times three times three times cosine of one hundred and thirty-five degrees, which works out to about three times the square root of two minus root two, roughly three point two four kilometers. <<WRITE_ANSWER:≈ 3.24 km|id=ans-3>> The key move was still the same: flip Q, find the new angle, apply the formula. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<WRITE_KEY:Subtraction = flip + add. Angle changes; formula stays the same.|id=key-2>> So remember: subtracting a vector is just addition with one vector turned around by one hundred and eighty degrees. That flip is the whole trick — and because it changes the angle between the vectors, the magnitude of the difference is generally different from the magnitude of the sum. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_4>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> If you're driving at sixty kilometers per hour north, and I told you to triple your speed — where are you going, and how fast? What if I said multiply by negative one? That second question is the interesting one. <<FOCUS:vector-a>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_4:scalar_mult_diagram>> <<SECTION:Scaling a vector|id=sec-1>>Let's set up our picture. Here's a vector called a, pointing to the right. It has some magnitude — call it a. <<TRACE:vector-a>> <<FOCUS:vector-3a>> <<WRITE_TEXT:b = k·a, k > 0: same direction, bigger|id=text-1>>Now multiply by three — a positive number. Watch what happens to the arrow. <<TRACE:vector-3a>> The new vector three a is three times as long, and it still points to the right. The direction didn't budge. Only the size changed. Multiplying a vector by a positive number scales its magnitude and keeps its direction exactly the same. <<POINT:vector-3a>> <<PAUSE:short>> The new vector b equals k times a, and its magnitude is just the absolute value of k multiplied by the magnitude of a. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{b} = k\vec{a}, \quad |\vec{b}| = |k| \cdot |\vec{a}||id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:vector-3a>> <<WRITE_KEY:Positive scalar → same direction, magnitude multiplied|id=key-1>>So doubling a vector doubles its length. Halving it shrinks it. The direction is untouched as long as the number stays positive. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now here's the real question: what happens if the number is negative? Say we multiply vector a by negative two. What do you think happens to the direction of the arrow? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:vector-neg2a>> <<WRITE_TEXT:k < 0: direction reverses|id=text-2>>Look — the new arrow points to the LEFT, and it's twice as long. The negative sign flipped the direction completely. <<TRACE:vector-neg2a>> Multiplying a vector by a negative number reverses its direction — and the magnitude is still scaled by the size of the number, ignoring the sign. <<POINT:vector-neg2a>> <<PAUSE:short>> The special case is multiplying by negative one. That just flips the arrow around — same length, exact opposite direction. The vectors a and negative a have equal magnitudes but point in opposite directions. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:unit-vector-u>> <<SECTION:Unit vectors|id=sec-2>>There's one more beautiful idea hiding here. Every vector has a direction. Can we separate the direction from the size cleanly? <<PAUSE:long>> Any vector a can be written as its magnitude a multiplied by u-hat, the unit vector pointing in its direction. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{a} = a\hat{u}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:u-hat: unit vector, magnitude = 1|id=text-3>>Yes — meet the unit vector, written as u-hat. It has magnitude exactly one, and it simply points in the direction of a. It carries pure direction, no size. <<TRACE:unit-vector-u>> <<POINT:unit-vector-u>> <<WRITE_KEY:Any vector: a = a · u-hat|id=key-2>>So any vector a is just its magnitude a — a plain number — multiplied by u-hat, which tells you which way to go. The magnitude and direction are neatly separated. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> That's the whole idea: a scalar times a vector is still a vector — same or opposite direction depending on the sign, and magnitude scaled by the size of that number. Simple rule, powerful tool.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_6>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> If you're pushing a lawnmower at an angle, does ALL of your push go forward — or does some of it get wasted pushing down into the ground? That question is exactly what vector resolution answers. <<SECTION:Resolution of Vectors|id=sec-1>> <<FOCUS:vector-oa>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_6:vector_resolution_diagram>> Let's draw a vector — call it a — starting at the origin O, pointing off at some angle in the X-Y plane. <<WRITE_TEXT:Vector a from origin O at angle alpha to X-axis|id=text-1>> The vector makes an angle alpha with the X-axis and an angle beta with the Y-axis. <<POINT:angle-alpha>> <<POINT:angle-alpha>> <<FOCUS:perp-ab>> Now drop a perpendicular from the tip of the vector — point A — straight down to the X-axis. It hits at point B. That length O-B is the shadow of your vector on the X-axis. We call it the projection onto X. <<TRACE:perp-ab>> <<FOCUS:perp-ac>> <<FOCUS:perp-ac>> Do the same thing sideways to the Y-axis — the foot lands at C, and O-C is the projection onto Y. Together, these two arrows O-B and O-C completely rebuild the original vector a. <<WRITE_TEXT:OA = OB + OC (vector addition)|id=text-2>> <<TRACE:perp-ac>> The vector equals its X-component times the unit vector i-hat, plus its Y-component times the unit vector j-hat. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{a} = a\cos\alpha\,\hat{i} + a\cos\beta\,\hat{j}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:component-ob>> <<FOCUS:component-ob>> Here's the key: using basic trigonometry in that right triangle, the length O-B equals a times cosine alpha, and O-C equals a times cosine beta. <<WRITE_KEY:x-component = a cos alpha, y-component = a cos beta|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:vector-oa>> So the full vector a, written with unit vectors i-hat along X and j-hat along Y, is: a equals a cosine alpha times i-hat plus a cosine beta times j-hat. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a = a\cos\alpha\,\hat{i} + a\cos\beta\,\hat{j}|id=eq-1>> <<POINT:vector-oa>> <<POINT:vector-oa>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Here's the beautiful thing — this idea generalises to any direction. The component of a vector along ANY direction is just the magnitude times the cosine of the angle it makes with that direction. <<WRITE_KEY:Component along direction = a cos(angle with that direction)|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Let's test that with a real example. A force of ten point five newtons acts on a particle at an angle of thirty-seven degrees from the vertical. How much of that force actually acts vertically? <<SECTION:Worked Example|id=sec-2>> <<WRITE_TEXT:F = 10.5 N, angle with vertical = 37°|id=text-3>> <<PAUSE:long>> The vertical component equals the force magnitude times the cosine of thirty-seven degrees, which is ten point five times four fifths, giving eight point four zero newtons. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F_{\text{vertical}} = F\cos\theta = 10.5 \times \frac{4}{5} = 8.40 \text{ N}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> The vertical component is the magnitude times cosine of the angle with the vertical. Cosine of thirty-seven degrees is four fifths, which equals zero point eight. So the vertical component equals ten point five times four fifths, which gives eight point four zero newtons. <<WRITE_STEP:F_vertical = F cos 37 = 10.5 × (4/5)|id=step-1>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:F_vertical = 8.40 N|id=ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Extended example one: a cyclist rides along a road that goes thirty degrees above horizontal. Their speed is twelve meters per second. How fast are they actually moving horizontally? The horizontal component of velocity is twelve times cosine of thirty degrees, which is twelve times zero point eight six six, giving about ten point four meters per second. <<SECTION:Extended Examples|id=sec-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:v_horizontal = 12 × cos 30 = 12 × 0.866 ≈ 10.4 m/s|id=step-2>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:v_horizontal ≈ 10.4 m/s|id=ans-2>> Extended example two: a delivery worker pulls a cart with a rope that makes an angle of sixty degrees with the horizontal, applying a force of twenty newtons. How much of that force is actually pulling the cart forward horizontally? <<WRITE_TEXT:Rope force = 20 N at 60° above horizontal|id=text-4>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The horizontal component is twenty times cosine of sixty degrees. Cosine of sixty degrees is one half, so the horizontal pull is twenty times one half, which equals ten newtons. Half the effort goes forward; the other half pulls the rope upward. <<WRITE_STEP:F_horizontal = 20 × cos 60 = 20 × 0.5 = 10 N|id=step-3>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:F_horizontal = 10 N|id=ans-3>> <<PAUSE:short>> So remember: resolving a vector means splitting it into perpendicular components using cosine. The component along any axis is always the magnitude times the cosine of the angle with that axis — and those two components, put back together, give you the original vector exactly. <<WRITE_KEY:Resolution: a = a cos(alpha) i-hat + a cos(beta) j-hat|id=key-3>>

<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:The Dot Product Idea|id=sec-1>>A weightlifter holds two hundred kilograms perfectly still above their head. Force? Enormous. Time? Minutes. Work done? Exactly zero. The reason is that force and motion have to line up — and measuring how much two vectors line up is precisely what the dot product does. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_7:dot_product_geometry>> <<WRITE_TEXT:dot product measures 'alignment' of two vectors|id=text-1>>Picture two vectors, a and b, both starting from the same point. The angle between them is theta. The dot product asks: out of all of b's length, how much of it is pointing in the same direction as a? <<TRACE:vector-a>> <<TRACE:vector-a>> <<FOCUS:projection-of-b-onto-a>> That 'shadow' of b onto a is the projection — it equals b times cosine of theta. So the dot product is just a times that shadow: a times b times cosine theta. <<TRACE:projection-of-b-onto-a>> <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> <<WRITE_TEXT:angle theta between the two vectors|id=text-2>>The angle theta lives right here, between the two vectors. The bigger the angle, the less they agree — and the smaller the dot product. The dot product is just the product of both magnitudes multiplied by the cosine of the angle between them — a single number. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = ab\cos\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:a · b = ab cosθ|id=eq-1>>So here it is: a dot b equals a times b times cosine of theta. <<WRITE_KEY:Result is a scalar — just a number, not a vector|id=key-1>>Notice — this gives us one plain number, not a new vector. That's why it's also called the scalar product. <<POINT:angle-theta>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:perpendicular-case-b>> <<SECTION:The Perpendicular Special Case|id=sec-2>>Now watch what happens when the two vectors are perfectly perpendicular — like these two. Theta is ninety degrees. Cosine of ninety degrees is zero. So the dot product is zero. <<POINT:perpendicular-case-b>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:perpendicular-label>> <<WRITE_TEXT:perpendicular vectors → dot product = 0|id=text-3>>The projection of one onto the other is zero — they share no common direction at all. They are completely 'ignoring' each other. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Worked Example — Negative Work|id=sec-3>>Let's make this real. A force of twelve newtons acts vertically upward on a particle. The particle is displaced two point zero meters vertically downward. What is the work done by the force? Work equals the dot product of force and displacement — magnitude of force times magnitude of displacement times cosine of the angle between them. <<WRITE_EQUATION:W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{r} = Fr\cos\theta|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_STEP:Identify the angle|id=step-1>>First, identify the angle between force and displacement. Force points straight up; displacement points straight down. They are in exactly opposite directions, so theta equals one hundred and eighty degrees. <<WRITE_STEP:Apply W = Fr cosθ|id=step-2>>Work W equals F dot r, which equals F times r times cosine of theta. Substituting: twelve newtons times two point zero meters times cosine of one hundred and eighty degrees. <<WRITE_STEP:cosine of 180° = −1|id=step-3>>Cosine of one hundred and eighty degrees equals negative one. So work equals twelve times two point zero times negative one. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:W = −24 J|id=ans-1>>Work done equals negative twenty-four joules. Negative! The force fought the displacement the entire way. The force tried to push the particle up; the particle moved down. That fight is captured by the negative sign — and the dot product gives us that automatically. <<SECTION:Extended Example 1 — Carrying Groceries|id=sec-4>>Here's one that surprises people. You carry your groceries home — holding the bag up with a force of twenty newtons — and you walk three meters horizontally to reach your door. The force is vertical; the motion is horizontal. How much work did you do on the bag? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:θ = 90°, so W = 0|id=step-4>>The force is straight up; the displacement is straight sideways — ninety degrees between them. Cosine of ninety degrees is zero. Work equals twenty times three times zero, which is zero joules. You carried the bag but did zero work on it in the physics sense. Your muscles were busy, but the bag gained no energy from your upward force. <<SECTION:Extended Example 2 — Cyclist and Crosswind|id=sec-5>>Now here's a genuine puzzle. A cyclist rides due east at steady speed. A strong wind blows from the south, pushing on them with a force of eight newtons — directly from the side. Does that sideways wind help the cyclist go faster, slow them down, or do neither? It feels like it should do something to their forward motion... <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Wind force ⊥ displacement → W = 0|id=step-5>>The wind force points north — perfectly perpendicular to the eastward displacement. Theta is ninety degrees, cosine is zero, work equals eight times any displacement times zero — always zero joules. <<WRITE_KEY:Perpendicular force → zero work, zero energy transfer|id=key-2>>The sideways wind does absolutely zero work on the cyclist's forward motion. It may tip them or push them off course, but it contributes nothing to speeding them up or slowing them down along their path. A force at ninety degrees is completely 'invisible' to the motion in that direction. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Wrap-Up|id=sec-6>>So the dot product is nature's built-in alignment detector. Two vectors perfectly aligned — maximum dot product. Perfectly opposite — dot product is negative. Perfectly perpendicular — dot product is exactly zero. One number, and it tells you everything about how two vectors cooperate. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_8>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_8:cross_product_diagram>> Point your fingers along a wall, curl them toward the floor — your thumb jabs sideways into empty air. You haven't touched the wall or the floor, yet something new appeared in a third direction entirely. That's the magic of the cross product: multiply two vectors and get a brand new vector pointing somewhere neither of the originals did. <<FOCUS:vector-a>> <<SECTION:The Cross Product — Two Vectors In, One New Vector Out|id=sec-1>>Here are two vectors, a and b, drawn tail to tail. <<WRITE_TEXT:a × b → a vector perpendicular to both|id=text-1>>Between them sits an angle theta — the smaller of the two angles you see at their tails. <<TRACE:vector-a>> <<FOCUS:cross-product-vector>> Now watch what happens when we form the cross product a cross b — a new arrow springs up, perpendicular to the flat surface that a and b share. It doesn't lie in the plane of a or b at all. <<TRACE:cross-product-vector>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> <<SECTION:Magnitude of the Cross Product|id=sec-2>>Here's the question: how big is that new vector? It depends on the angle theta between a and b. <<POINT:angle-theta>> <<PAUSE:long>> The size of the new vector you get is just the two magnitudes multiplied together, then scaled by the sine of the angle between them. <<WRITE_EQUATION:|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = ab\sin\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = ab\sin\theta|id=eq-1>>The magnitude of the cross product is a times b times sine of theta. If the two vectors are parallel, theta is zero, sine of zero is zero, and the cross product vanishes — parallel vectors produce nothing. Push them to ninety degrees and sine of theta hits one, giving you the largest possible result. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:right-hand-label>> <<SECTION:Direction — The Right-Hand Thumb Rule|id=sec-3>>Now for direction. Stretch your right hand flat, fingers pointing along a. Curl those fingers toward b. <<WRITE_TEXT:Right-hand thumb rule: fingers a→b, thumb = a×b|id=text-2>>Your thumb now points exactly where the cross product arrow goes. <<POINT:right-hand-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> Notice: if you swap the order and compute b cross a instead, your fingers would curl the other way, and the thumb flips direction. That's why a cross b is not the same as b cross a — the cross product cares about order. <<POINT:cross-product-vector>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Worked Example|id=sec-4>>Let's use this. Vector A has a magnitude of five units, vector B has a magnitude of six units, and the magnitude of A cross B is fifteen units. What is the angle between them? <<PAUSE:long>> <<WRITE_STEP:| A × B | = A × B × sinθ|id=step-1>>We write the magnitude formula: the magnitude of A cross B equals A times B times sine of theta. We know the magnitude of A cross B is fifteen units, A is five units, B is six units. <<WRITE_STEP:15 = 5 × 6 × sinθ|id=step-2>>So we plug in: fifteen equals five times six times sine of theta. Five times six is thirty, so fifteen equals thirty times sine of theta. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:sinθ = 15/30 = 1/2|id=step-3>>Dividing both sides by thirty gives sine of theta equals one half. And sine equals one half for two angles — <<WRITE_ANSWER:θ = 30° or 150°|id=ans-1>>theta equals thirty degrees, or theta equals one hundred fifty degrees. Both are valid answers! <<SECTION:Extended Example 1 — Cricket|id=sec-5>>A cricket bat swings through an angle and strikes the ball. The bat velocity vector points forward — magnitude four meters per second — and the ball's spin axis vector points upward — magnitude three meters per second. The cross product magnitude is four times three times sine of ninety degrees, which is twelve meters squared per second squared. The swing and the spin axis are perfectly perpendicular, so sine of ninety is one — maximum cross product! <<SECTION:Extended Example 2 — Door Hinge|id=sec-6>>You push a door open. Your force vector has magnitude six newtons, pointing horizontally away from the hinge. The door's length vector has magnitude two meters, also pointing horizontally but at sixty degrees to your force. The torque — which is a cross product — has magnitude six times two times sine of sixty degrees. Sine of sixty degrees is root three over two, roughly zero point eight seven, so the torque magnitude is roughly ten point four newton meters. <<WRITE_KEY:Torque = r × F — a real cross product!|id=key-1>>That torque is what rotates the door — and by the right-hand rule it points along the hinge axis, which is exactly where a door rotates. <<WRITE_KEY:Cross product: magnitude = ab sinθ, direction by right-hand rule|id=key-2>>So here's what to lock in: the cross product of two vectors gives a new vector whose size is a times b times sine of theta, and whose direction — perpendicular to both — is found by pointing your right-hand fingers along the first vector, curling toward the second, and reading your thumb. That thumb is always your answer. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_9>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_9:tangent_slope_diagram>> If a car is speeding up, how fast is it speeding up right now — not over the last minute, not over the last second, but at this exact instant? That single question is what differential calculus was invented to answer. <<SECTION:The Derivative — Instantaneous Rate of Change|id=sec-1>> <<TRACE:curve-main>> <<FOCUS:point-A>> Say y and x are two quantities linked together — every x gives exactly one y. Their graph is some curve. Pick any point A on it. Now nudge x by a small amount called delta x, and y shifts by a corresponding delta y. <<WRITE_TEXT:delta y / delta x = slope of secant AB|id=text-1>> <<POINT:point-A>> <<FOCUS:secant-AB>> The ratio delta y over delta x is the slope of the straight line AB connecting A to its neighbour B — a secant line cutting across the curve. But this is only a rough average rate; the curve may be steeper at B than at A. <<TRACE:secant-AB>> So here's the key question: what if we dragged point B closer and closer to A — making delta x smaller and smaller, all the way to zero? What does that secant line turn into? <<POINT:point-B>> <<POINT:point-B>> <<PAUSE:long>> As the gap between the two points shrinks to zero, the slope of the secant line becomes the slope of the tangent — and that limiting ratio is exactly what we call the derivative. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{dy}{dx} = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:tangent-at-x2>> It becomes the tangent line — the line that just grazes the curve at A without crossing it. <<WRITE_KEY:dy/dx = slope of tangent at a point|id=key-1>> The derivative dy over dx is exactly that limiting slope: the instantaneous rate of change of y with respect to x at the point A. That is the most important idea in this entire topic. <<TRACE:tangent-at-x2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:tangent-at-x2>> Now let's read derivatives straight off a graph. <<SECTION:Reading Slopes from a Graph|id=sec-2>> The curve in front of us rises, peaks, and falls. At x equals two, the tangent line is labelled AC. It has a rise of five and a run of four, so its slope is five over four. Therefore dy over dx equals five over four at x equals two. <<POINT:tangent-at-x2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:tangent-at-x6>> At x equals six we're at the very top of the hill. The tangent lies perfectly flat — parallel to the horizontal axis. A horizontal line has slope zero, so dy over dx equals zero at x equals six. <<WRITE_TEXT:x = 6 → dy/dx = 0 (flat peak)|id=text-2>> <<FOCUS:tangent-at-x10>> At x equals ten the curve is falling. The tangent line DF has a rise of negative five and a run of four — it slopes downward. So dy over dx equals negative five over four at x equals ten. Rising curve means positive derivative; falling curve means negative derivative. <<WRITE_TEXT:x = 10 → dy/dx = −5/4 (falling)|id=text-3>> <<POINT:tangent-at-x10>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Graphs are powerful, but we also need to find derivatives algebraically. <<SECTION:Algebraic Method — The Square Example|id=sec-3>> Take a square with side length L. Its area is A equals L squared. Now increase the side from L to L plus delta L. What does the area become? <<PAUSE:long>> As delta L shrinks to zero, two L plus delta L collapses to just two L — so the derivative of A with respect to L is two L. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{dA}{dL} = \lim_{\Delta L \to 0} \frac{\Delta A}{\Delta L} = 2L|id=eq-2|boxed>> The new area is L plus delta L, all squared. Expanding: L squared plus two L times delta L plus delta L squared. The original area was just L squared, so the change in area, delta A, equals two L times delta L plus delta L squared. <<WRITE_STEP:A + ΔA = (L + ΔL)² = L² + 2L·ΔL + (ΔL)²|id=step-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:ΔA = 2L·ΔL + (ΔL)²|id=step-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> Divide both sides by delta L: the ratio delta A over delta L equals two L plus delta L. <<WRITE_STEP:ΔA/ΔL = 2L + ΔL|id=step-3>> Now let delta L shrink toward zero — that leftover delta L vanishes, and we're left with exactly two L. So the derivative of A with respect to L is two L. <<WRITE_ANSWER:dA/dL = 2L|id=ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> The product rule says: differentiate one factor and keep the other, then swap — differentiate the other and keep the first — and add the two results. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{d}{dx}(uv) = u\frac{dv}{dx} + v\frac{du}{dx}|id=eq-3|boxed>> That process — expand, form the ratio, take the limit — is the universal recipe for any derivative. <<SECTION:Product Rule|id=sec-4>> Now, what if y is a product of two functions, like y equals e to the x times sine x? We can't just differentiate them separately and multiply. The product rule handles this. It says: the derivative of u times v equals u times the derivative of v, plus v times the derivative of u. <<WRITE_TEXT:Product rule: (uv)' = u·v' + v·u'|id=text-4>> Think of it as: keep the first, differentiate the second — then keep the second, differentiate the first — and add. Applying the product rule to e to the x times sine x, we collect the two pieces and factor out e to the x. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{dy}{dx} = e^x(\cos x + \sin x)|id=eq-4|boxed>> Applying this to y equals e to the x times sine x: let u equal e to the x and v equal sine x. The derivative of sine x is cosine x, and the derivative of e to the x is e to the x. <<WRITE_STEP:dy/dx = e^x · cos x + sin x · e^x|id=step-4>> Factoring out e to the x, the final answer is e to the x times the quantity cosine x plus sine x. <<WRITE_ANSWER:dy/dx = e^x(cos x + sin x)|id=ans-2>> Neat — two known derivatives combined by one rule. <<SECTION:Extended Example — Water Filling a Tank|id=sec-5>> Here's a real-world one. Water pours into a cylindrical tank and the depth d in metres after t minutes is d equals three t squared. How fast is the depth rising at exactly t equals two minutes? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Use the algebraic method: replace t with t plus delta t, expand, subtract the original, divide by delta t, then let delta t go to zero. <<WRITE_STEP:d + Δd = 3(t + Δt)² = 3t² + 6t·Δt + 3(Δt)²|id=step-5>> <<WRITE_STEP:Δd/Δt = 6t + 3Δt → 6t as Δt→0|id=step-6>> So d d over d t equals six t. At t equals two, the depth is rising at six times two, which is twelve metres per minute. <<WRITE_ANSWER:dd/dt = 6t → at t=2: 12 metres per minute|id=ans-3>> <<WRITE_KEY:Derivative = instantaneous rate of change = slope of tangent|id=key-2>> So to sum up: the derivative dy over dx is the slope of the tangent to the curve at that point. It's positive when the curve rises, zero at a peak or trough, and negative when it falls. And you find it by forming the ratio of tiny changes and letting those changes vanish — that limit is the heartbeat of calculus. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_10>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> You throw a ball straight up — at the very top of its path, is it speeding up, slowing down, or something else entirely? Think about it. At that exact peak, the ball is doing neither. For one tiny instant, it has stopped rising and hasn't yet started falling. Its velocity is zero. And that zero is the key to everything we're about to learn. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_10:maxmin_curve>> <<SECTION:Maxima and Minima|id=sec-1>>Let's look at a curve. Here's y plotted against x — it climbs to a peak, then dips to a valley. <<TRACE:curve-y-x>> <<FOCUS:tangent-at-max>> At the very top — the maximum — draw a tangent line. It's perfectly horizontal. And at the bottom — the minimum — the tangent is horizontal again. <<WRITE_TEXT:Tangent at max and min is horizontal|id=text-1>> <<TRACE:tangent-at-max>> <<TRACE:tangent-at-max>> At the peak or the trough, the curve is momentarily flat — its slope, which is the derivative, is exactly zero. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{dy}{dx} = 0|id=eq-1|boxed>> A horizontal line has a slope of zero. And the slope of a curve at any point is just its derivative, d y by d x. <<WRITE_KEY:At max or min: dy/dx = 0|id=key-1>>So here is the golden rule — at any maximum or minimum, the first derivative equals zero. <<POINT:tangent-at-min>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:point-maximum>> But here's the real question — if d y by d x equals zero at BOTH the maximum and the minimum, how do we tell them apart? <<PAUSE:long>> If the slope is falling through zero, it's a maximum; if the slope is rising through zero, it's a minimum — that's exactly what the second derivative measures. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} < 0 \text{ (maximum)}, \quad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} > 0 \text{ (minimum)}|id=eq-2|boxed>> Watch the slope as you walk along the curve. Before the maximum, the curve is rising — slope is positive. Right at the top, slope is zero. Just after, the curve is falling — slope goes negative. <<WRITE_TEXT:Before max: slope positive → zero → negative|id=text-2>>So the slope is decreasing through zero. That means the rate of change of the slope — the second derivative — is negative at a maximum. <<POINT:slope-positive-region>> <<POINT:slope-positive-region>> <<PAUSE:short>> The height of the ball at any time t is given by initial speed times time, minus one half times g times t squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:h = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^2|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<FOCUS:slope-negative-region>> At the minimum, the opposite is true. The slope goes from negative, through zero, to positive — it's increasing. So the second derivative is positive at a minimum. <<WRITE_KEY:d²y/dx² < 0 → maximum; d²y/dx² > 0 → minimum|id=key-2>>That's your complete toolkit: first derivative zero to find the point, second derivative to label it. <<POINT:slope-negative-region>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Book Example — Ball Thrown Upward|id=sec-2>>Now let's use this. A ball is thrown straight up with initial speed u. Its height h at time t is given by h equals u times t minus one half times g times t squared, where g equals nine point eight meters per second squared and is a constant. We want the time at which the ball reaches maximum height. Setting the derivative of height equal to zero and solving gives us the exact time when the ball is at its highest point. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{dh}{dt} = u - gt = 0 \implies t = \frac{u}{g}|id=eq-4|boxed>> We know maximum height occurs when d h by d t equals zero. So let's differentiate. <<WRITE_STEP:Differentiate h = ut − ½gt²|id=step-1>>The derivative of u times t with respect to t is just u. The derivative of one half g t squared is one half times g times two t, which simplifies to g times t. <<WRITE_STEP:dh/dt = u − gt|id=step-2>>So d h by d t equals u minus g times t. Now we set this equal to zero for maximum height. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:u − gt = 0 → t = u/g|id=step-3>>Setting u minus g times t equal to zero gives t equals u divided by g. <<WRITE_ANSWER:t = u / g|id=ans-1>>That is the exact time the ball reaches its peak — a clean, simple answer straight from the condition that the first derivative equals zero. <<SECTION:Extended Example 1 — Profit Curve|id=sec-3>>Let's try another scenario. A small food stall finds that its daily profit P in rupees depends on the number of items x it sells, following P equals sixty times x minus three times x squared. At what number of items is profit maximised? <<WRITE_STEP:dP/dx = 60 − 6x|id=step-4>>We differentiate: d P by d x equals sixty minus six times x. Set that equal to zero — sixty minus six times x equals zero, so x equals ten. <<WRITE_ANSWER:x = 10 items|id=ans-2>>The stall maximises profit at ten items sold per day. <<SECTION:Extended Example 2 — Cooling Tea|id=sec-4>>One more. The temperature T of a cup of tea in degrees Celsius, measured t minutes after being poured, follows T equals eighty minus four times t plus point one times t squared, for t between zero and twenty. When is the tea at its coolest in that window? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:dT/dt = −4 + 0.2t|id=step-5>>Differentiate: d T by d t equals negative four plus point two times t. Set equal to zero: point two times t equals four, so t equals twenty minutes. <<WRITE_ANSWER:t = 20 min (minimum temperature)|id=ans-3>>The second derivative is positive — it's a minimum — so the tea is coldest at twenty minutes. The derivative gave us the answer instantly, no guesswork needed. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_11>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_11:area_under_curve>> What if I told you that slicing something into infinitely many thin pieces — and then adding them all back together — is one of the most powerful tricks in all of physics? That is literally what integration is. <<SECTION:Integral Calculus — Area Under a Curve|id=sec-1>> <<TRACE:curve-pq>> <<FOCUS:region-pabq>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Area under curve = region between curve, x-axis, and two vertical lines|id=text-1>>Look at this curve running from point P above x equals a, to point Q above x equals b. The shaded region trapped between the curve, the x-axis, and those two vertical edges — that is the area we want to find. <<TRACE:region-pabq>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the clever trick: fill that region with thin rectangular bars, side by side. Each bar has a small width — call it delta x — and its height is just the value of the curve at that point. We add up all those little areas. <<TRACE:rect-bars>> <<POINT:rect-bars>> The total area of all the bars is just the sum of each bar's height times its width — we can write that compactly with a sigma symbol. <<WRITE_EQUATION:I' = \sum_{i=1}^{N} f(x_i)\,\Delta x|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:delta-x-label>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:I' = \sum f(x_i)\,\Delta x|id=eq-1>>The total area of all the bars is the sum of height times width for every bar. We write that as I-prime equals the sum of f of x-i times delta x. When we let the number of bars grow without limit, the sum becomes perfect — and we write that perfect sum with a stretched S called the integral sign. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^{N} f(x_i)\,\Delta x|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:rect-bars>> Now here is the key question: what happens as we make the bars thinner and thinner — as delta x shrinks toward zero and the number of bars shoots toward infinity? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> <<WRITE_KEY:Definite integral = exact area under curve (infinite thin bars)|id=key-1>>The bars fit the curve more and more perfectly. In the limit, the sum becomes exact — it equals the true area. We call this the definite integral, written with a stretched S from a to b. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\int_a^b f(x)\,dx|id=eq-2>> The definite integral of a curve from a to b is the exact area under that curve, found by adding infinitely many infinitely thin rectangular bars. <<TRACE:curve-pq>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:rect-bars>> <<SECTION:Book Example — Trapezium: y = x|id=sec-2>>Let us prove this with a real shape. The curve is y equals x — a straight line through the origin. The area between x equals a and x equals b is a trapezium. We divide it into N rectangular bars, each of width delta x equals b minus a divided by N. After summing the arithmetic series and letting delta x shrink to zero, the area of the trapezium comes out to exactly one half times b squared minus a squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\int_a^b x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}(b^2 - a^2)|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<WRITE_STEP:Heights: a, a+Δx, a+2Δx, …, a+(N−1)Δx|id=step-1>>The heights of the bars are a, then a plus delta x, then a plus two delta x, all the way up to a plus N minus one times delta x. These heights form an arithmetic progression. <<POINT:point-p>> <<WRITE_STEP:Sum of AP: S = (N/2)(first + last) = (N/2)(a + b − Δx)|id=step-2>>We use the arithmetic series formula: S equals n over two times the quantity first term plus last term. The first height is a and the last is b minus delta x, so S equals N over two times a plus b minus delta x. <<FOCUS:region-pabq>> <<WRITE_STEP:I' = S·Δx = (N/2)(a + b − Δx)·Δx|id=step-3>>Multiply through by delta x to get the total bar area. Then as delta x shrinks to zero, the term containing delta x vanishes. We are left with N times delta x equals b minus a, so the whole expression simplifies. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:\int_a^b x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}(b^2 - a^2)|id=ans-1>>The final result: the integral of x from a to b equals one half times b squared minus a squared. And we can check this instantly — the antiderivative of x is one half x squared, differentiate it and you get x right back. <<WRITE_TEXT:Antiderivative of x → ½x², d/dx(½x²) = x ✓|id=text-2>> <<TRACE:curve-pq>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Power Rule Shortcut|id=sec-3>>That antiderivative shortcut is the real superpower. To find the antiderivative of x to the power n, you raise the power by one and divide by the new power. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}|id=eq-3>> To evaluate a definite integral: find the antiderivative, plug in the upper limit, plug in the lower limit, and subtract. <<PAUSE:short>> Applying the antiderivative of each term and evaluating at the two limits, we subtract the lower result from the upper result to get the final answer. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\int_3^6 (2x^2 + 3x + 5)\,dx = \left[\frac{2}{3}x^3 + \frac{3}{2}x^2 + 5x\right]_3^6 = 181.5|id=eq-4|boxed>> <<SECTION:Worked Example — Polynomial Integral|id=sec-4>>Now let us apply this. Evaluate the integral from three to six of two x squared plus three x plus five, with respect to x. First, we use the sum rule and split it into three separate integrals. <<WRITE_STEP:∫(2x²+3x+5)dx = ∫2x² dx + ∫3x dx + ∫5 dx|id=step-4>> <<WRITE_STEP:Antiderivatives: (2/3)x³ + (3/2)x² + 5x|id=step-5>>The antiderivative of two x squared is two thirds x cubed. The antiderivative of three x is three halves x squared. The antiderivative of five is five x. Put them together. <<WRITE_STEP:At x=6: (2/3)(216) + (3/2)(36) + 5(6)|id=step-6>>Now evaluate at x equals six: two thirds times two hundred sixteen, plus three halves times thirty six, plus five times six. <<WRITE_STEP:At x=3: (2/3)(27) + (3/2)(9) + 5(3)|id=step-7>>Then evaluate at x equals three: two thirds times twenty seven, plus three halves times nine, plus five times three. Now subtract the lower from the upper. <<WRITE_STEP:(2/3)(216−27) = 126 | (3/2)(36−9) = 40.5 | 5(6−3) = 15|id=step-8>>Two thirds times the quantity two hundred sixteen minus twenty seven gives one hundred twenty six. Three halves times the quantity thirty six minus nine gives forty point five. Five times the quantity six minus three gives fifteen. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:126 + 40.5 + 15 = 181.5|id=ans-2>>Add them up: one hundred twenty six plus forty point five plus fifteen equals one hundred eighty one point five. That is the exact area under the curve between three and six. <<SECTION:Extended Example 1 — Water Filling a Tank|id=sec-5>>Real-world anchor: water flows into a tank and the flow rate in litres per second is given by v equals two t, where t is time in seconds. How much water enters between t equals one and t equals three seconds? That is just the integral of two t from one to three. <<WRITE_STEP:∫₁³ 2t dt = [t²]₁³|id=step-9>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:[t²]₁³ = 9 − 1 = 8 litres|id=ans-3>>The antiderivative of two t is t squared. Evaluate at t equals three: nine. Evaluate at t equals one: one. Subtract — eight litres of water entered the tank. Simple. <<SECTION:Extended Example 2 — Braking Car|id=sec-6>>A car brakes and its speed in meters per second is v equals twelve minus four t. How far does it travel from t equals zero to t equals three seconds before stopping? Distance is the integral of velocity with respect to time. <<WRITE_STEP:∫₀³ (12−4t) dt = [12t − 2t²]₀³|id=step-10>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:[12t − 2t²]₀³ = 36 − 18 = 18 metres|id=ans-4>>At t equals three: twelve times three minus two times nine equals thirty six minus eighteen equals eighteen. At t equals zero: zero. The car travels eighteen metres while braking. <<WRITE_KEY:To evaluate: antiderivative → plug in limits → subtract|id=key-2>> To evaluate a definite integral — find the antiderivative, plug in the upper limit, plug in the lower limit, and subtract. Every time. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> You measure a pencil and say it's ten point four six centimetres long. Your friend just says it's about ten centimetres. Who's being more honest about what they actually know? The answer depends on the instrument — and that's exactly what significant digits are about. <<FOCUS:scale-body>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_12:metre_scale_reading>> <<SECTION:What are Significant Digits?|id=sec-1>>Every time you measure something, you're reading a calibrated scale — a ruler, an ammeter, a thermometer. Some digits you can read with complete confidence. Then there's one final digit you have to estimate — your best eye-guess within the smallest gap on the scale. That smallest gap is called the least count of the instrument. <<WRITE_TEXT:Least count = smallest subdivision on scale|id=text-1>>On a metre scale, the major markings are every centimetre, and between each centimetre there are ten smaller divisions. So the least count — the smallest subdivision — is one millimetre. <<TRACE:scale-body>> <<FOCUS:object-edge>> Now here's the classic example. One end of an object is placed at the zero mark. The other end falls somewhere between the ten point four centimetre mark and the ten point five centimetre mark. We can't read beyond millimetres directly — so we mentally divide that one millimetre gap into ten parts and guess where the edge lands. We note the reading as ten point four six centimetres. <<POINT:object-edge>> The reading ten point four six centimetres has three certain digits — one, zero, four — and one doubtful digit, six. All four together are the significant digits. <<WRITE_EQUATION:10.46 \text{ cm} = \underbrace{1,\, 0,\, 4}_{\text{certain}} + \underbrace{6}_{\text{doubtful}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:certain-digits-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:Significant digits = certain digits + one doubtful digit|id=key-1>>The digits one, zero, and four — we read those straight off the scale. They are certain. But the six? That came from our eye estimation. It is the doubtful digit. Together, one, zero, four, and six are all four significant digits of this measurement. <<POINT:certain-digits-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:doubtful-digit-label>> Notice the six is not wrong — it's our best honest guess. We report it because it carries real information, even if it carries a small uncertainty. That's the whole philosophy: significant digits are about being honest about how much your instrument actually told you. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:The Tricky Case — Trailing Zeros|id=sec-2>>Here's a question that trips everyone up. If I write a measurement as six hundred millimetres, how many significant digits does that have? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:600 mm — ambiguous without context|id=text-2>>It depends entirely on the instrument used. If the scale only had markings at every metre, then six is the only digit obtained by reading — the two zeros are just placeholders. Only one significant digit. But if the scale had centimetre markings, then the six and the first zero were both read off the scale — two significant digits. And if the scale had millimetre markings, all three digits six, zero, zero were read — three significant digits. Same number, three completely different meanings. <<PAUSE:short>> The same six hundred millimetres can mean one, two, or three significant digits depending on the instrument — scientific notation shows exactly which zeros count. <<WRITE_EQUATION:600 \text{ mm} \rightarrow 6 \times 10^2 \text{ mm},\quad 6.0 \times 10^2 \text{ mm},\quad 6.00 \times 10^2 \text{ mm}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Use scientific notation to remove ambiguity|id=text-3>>To avoid this confusion, we use scientific notation. Six times ten squared millimetres means only one significant digit. Six point zero times ten squared millimetres means two. Six point zero zero times ten squared millimetres means three. The zeros after the decimal point in scientific notation are never placeholders — they always count. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Zeros After the Decimal — Two Rules|id=sec-3>>Now what about zeros in small decimals? Consider zero point zero zero two three. Are any of those zeros significant? <<PAUSE:long>> Leading zeros after the decimal in a number less than one are not significant, but zeros sandwiched between non-zero digits always are. <<WRITE_EQUATION:0.0023 \rightarrow 2 \text{ sig. digits};\qquad 1.0023 \rightarrow 5 \text{ sig. digits}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:0.0023 → 2 sig. digits; 1.0023 → 5 sig. digits|id=text-4>>No — those leading zeros are only there to show the size of the number. Only two and three are significant. So zero point zero zero two three has just two significant digits. But now look at one point zero zero two three. Those zeros are sandwiched between non-zero digits — they were genuinely measured. All five digits are significant. <<SECTION:Real-World Example — Cooking|id=sec-4>>Here's a quick real-world check. You're following a recipe that says add zero point zero five litres of vanilla extract. How many significant digits is that? The leading zeros after the decimal are just place-holders — only the five is significant. One significant digit. But if the bottle label says zero point zero five zero litres, that trailing zero after the five was measured — it means the instrument was precise enough to confirm the measurement isn't zero point zero four nine or zero point zero five one. Now there are two significant digits. Same quantity, different instruments, different honesty. <<WRITE_KEY:Scientific notation = unambiguous significant digits|id=key-2>>So here's the takeaway you must carry forward. Every measurement has significant digits — the ones your instrument actually earned. Certain digits you read directly, one doubtful digit you estimate, and that's it. Any zeros that are just holding a place don't count. When in doubt, scientific notation tells the truth immediately. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> You measure two masses — twelve point zero kilograms and seven point zero kilograms — punch them into a calculator, and it spits back one point seven one four two eight five dot dot dot. Eight digits from two rough measurements. Which of those digits can you actually trust? <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:The Division/Multiplication Rule|id=sec-1>>Here's the key insight. The zero in twelve point zero is a doubtful digit — it's the last digit someone read off a scale. Same for the zero in seven point zero. So the answer can't possibly be more reliable than the shakiest number going in. Seven point zero has only two significant digits, so the answer must also have only two significant digits. <<PAUSE:short>> Twelve point zero has three significant digits and seven point zero has two, so the answer can only keep two significant digits — one point seven. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{12.0}{7.0} = 1.7|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Multiply/divide → keep fewest sig. digits|id=key-1>>That's the rule for multiplication and division: the answer has as many significant digits as the number with the fewest significant digits. Twelve point zero divided by seven point zero rounds to one point seven — not one point seven one four two eight five. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Rounding rules|id=sec-2>>Before we apply this to bigger calculations, let's nail down exactly how to round. Four cases — rounding to three significant digits. <<WRITE_TEXT:Round to 3 sig. digits|id=text-1>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<WRITE_STEP:15462 → next digit after 3rd sig. dig. is 6 > 5 → round up → 15500|id=step-1>>First: fifteen thousand four hundred sixty-two. The third significant digit is four. The digit right after it is six, which is greater than five, so we round the four up to five and replace the rest with zeros. Result: fifteen thousand five hundred. <<WRITE_STEP:14.745 → next digit is 4 < 5 → leave unchanged → 14.7|id=step-2>>Second: fourteen point seven four five. The third significant digit is seven. The digit after it is four, which is less than five — so seven stays as it is. Result: fourteen point seven. <<WRITE_STEP:14.750 → next digit is 5, 7 is odd → round up → 14.8|id=step-3>>Third: fourteen point seven five zero. The next digit is exactly five — the borderline case. We look at the digit being rounded — seven. Seven is odd, so we round it up. Result: fourteen point eight. <<WRITE_STEP:14.650 × 10^12 → next digit is 5, 6 is even → leave unchanged → 14.6 × 10^12|id=step-4>>Fourth: fourteen point six five zero times ten to the power twelve. Next digit is again five. This time the digit being rounded is six — even — so we leave it unchanged. Result: fourteen point six times ten to the power twelve. The rule when the next digit is exactly five: round to even. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Multiplication example|id=sec-3>>Now a full multiplication-and-division problem. Evaluate twenty-five point two times one thousand three hundred seventy-four divided by thirty-three point three. Before touching a calculator — how many significant digits should the answer have? <<PAUSE:long>> The raw calculator answer is one thousand thirty-nine point seven eight three eight and so on, but we round to three significant digits, giving one thousand and forty. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{25.2 \times 1374}{33.3} = 1040|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_STEP:25.2 → 3 sig. dig. | 1374 → 4 sig. dig. | 33.3 → 3 sig. dig.|id=step-5>>Twenty-five point two has three significant digits. One thousand three hundred seventy-four has four. Thirty-three point three has three. The minimum is three — so the answer must have three significant digits. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Raw result = 1039.7838…|id=step-6>>The calculator gives one thousand thirty-nine point seven eight three eight and so on. We need to round that to three significant digits. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:25.2 × 1374 ÷ 33.3 = 1040|id=ans-1>>The third significant digit is nine. The digit after it is seven — greater than five — so nine rounds up to ten, which carries over. The answer is one thousand and forty. Notice the zero at the end is a placeholder, not a significant digit. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_13:sig_fig_column_diagram>> <<SECTION:Addition rule|id=sec-4>>Addition and subtraction work differently. The question isn't how many significant digits each number has — it's which column first becomes unreliable. Let's add twenty-four point three six, zero point zero six two three, and two hundred fifty-six point two. <<FOCUS:doubtful-column-line>> <<WRITE_KEY:Add/subtract → drop digits right of first doubtful column|id=key-2>>Line them up at the decimal point. Two hundred fifty-six point two has its last written digit — and its doubtful digit — in the tenths column. That makes the tenths column the first doubtful column. Everything to the right of it is unreliable, no matter what the other numbers say. <<TRACE:doubtful-column-line>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rounded-24p4>> So we round each number to the tenths place before adding. Twenty-four point three six becomes twenty-four point four. Zero point zero six two three becomes zero point one. Two hundred fifty-six point two stays as it is. <<TRACE:rounded-24p4>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:final-sum>> <<WRITE_STEP:256.2 + 24.4 + 0.1 = 280.7|id=step-7>>Now add: two hundred fifty-six point two plus twenty-four point four plus zero point one equals two hundred eighty point seven. That's our answer — reliable to the tenths column, no further. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Extended example 1 — cooking|id=sec-5>>Imagine you're scaling a recipe. You measure three point five grams of salt and two point one five grams of pepper. How many significant digits should their combined mass have? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:3.5 → doubtful in tenths | 2.15 → doubtful in hundredths → drop hundredths|id=step-8>>Three point five has its doubtful digit in the tenths column. Two point one five has its doubtful digit in the hundredths column — but that's further right than the tenths. So we drop the hundredths and round two point one five to two point two. One decimal place — that's as far as our scales can be trusted. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Extended example 2 — speed|id=sec-6>>A cyclist covers a distance of four point two kilometers in a time of zero point two five hours.
