<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> You measure the same object ten times with the same ruler and get ten slightly different answers. Which one is right? <<SECTION:Types of Experimental Error|id=sec-1>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:2_14:error_distribution>> <<WRITE_TEXT:3 sources: faulty equipment, carelessness, random|id=text-1>>There are three sources of error in any experiment. Faulty equipment — like a bent ruler. Carelessness — like reading a scale from an angle. And random errors, which have no single identifiable cause. The first two you can hunt down and fix. Random errors? You cannot eliminate them. <<TRACE:data-dots>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:mean-line>> <<WRITE_KEY:Random errors can't be removed — average many results to approach the true value|id=key-1>>Here is the trick with random errors: sometimes they push your reading a little too high, sometimes a little too low. So when you repeat the experiment many times and average the results, the positive and negative errors tend to cancel out — and your average lands very close to the true value. <<TRACE:mean-line>> <<PAUSE:short>> The best estimate of the true value is just the ordinary average: add all the results and divide by the number of observations. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\bar{x} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:true-value-line>> <<SECTION:Standard Deviation|id=sec-2>>But how close is close? We need a number that captures the spread — the uncertainty. That number is called the standard deviation, sigma. The best estimate of the true value is just the plain average, x-bar. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\bar{x} = \frac{1}{N}\sum x_i|id=eq-1>>Add all your measurements and divide by N — that is x-bar, your best guess at the true value. <<POINT:mean-line>> The spread is captured by the standard deviation sigma: take each measurement's distance from the mean, square it, average those squared distances, then take the square root. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:sigma-band>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2}|id=eq-2>>Then sigma measures how far the individual readings stray from that average. Square each gap, average the squares, take the square root. That shaded band on the diagram — x-bar plus or minus sigma — is where the true value almost certainly lives. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:True value lies within x-bar ± sigma|id=key-2>>In fact, there is a ninety-five percent chance the true value is within x-bar plus or minus one point nine six sigma. Use x-bar plus or minus three sigma if you want ninety-nine percent confidence. Either way, sigma is your honest label on how uncertain the answer is. <<POINT:sigma-band>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Worked Example — Focal Length of a Concave Mirror|id=sec-3>>Let us work this out with real data. A student measures the focal length of a concave mirror ten times. The readings in centimeters are: twenty-five point four, twenty-five point two, twenty-five point six, twenty-five point one, twenty-five point three, twenty-five point two, twenty-five point five, twenty-five point four, twenty-five point three, and twenty-five point four. <<WRITE_STEP:Sum = 25.4+25.2+25.6+25.1+25.3+25.2+25.5+25.4+25.3+25.4 = 253.4 cm|id=step-1>>First, the average. Add all ten readings: the total is two hundred fifty-three point four centimeters. Divide by ten observations. <<WRITE_STEP:x-bar = 253.4 / 10 = 25.34 cm|id=step-2>>x-bar equals twenty-five point three four centimeters. That is the best value of focal length from these experiments. <<WRITE_STEP:Deviations squared then summed|id=step-3>>Now for sigma. For each reading, subtract twenty-five point three four, square the result, then add all ten squared deviations together. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:sigma = sqrt(sum of squared deviations / 10) ≈ 0.14 cm|id=step-4>>Divide that sum by ten and take the square root. The standard deviation sigma comes out to approximately zero point one four centimeters. So the result is reported as twenty-five point three four plus or minus zero point one four centimeters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:f = (25.34 ± 0.14) cm|id=ans-1>>The focal length is twenty-five point three four plus or minus zero point one four centimeters. That plus or minus is not a guess — it is sigma, the mathematically honest statement of uncertainty. <<SECTION:Extended Example 1 — Timing a Pendulum|id=sec-4>>Now imagine you are timing one complete swing of a pendulum in a lab. You do it eight times and get these times in seconds: one point nine two, one point eight eight, one point nine five, one point nine zero, one point eight seven, one point nine three, one point nine one, one point nine zero. What is the best value and its uncertainty? Same process: sum is fifteen point two six seconds, divide by eight — average is one point nine zero seven five seconds, roughly one point nine one seconds. Compute sigma the same way. You would find sigma is about zero point zero two seconds, so your answer is one point nine one plus or minus zero point zero two seconds. <<SECTION:Extended Example 2 — Weighing Spice in a Kitchen|id=sec-5>>A home cook is calibrating a digital kitchen scale by repeatedly weighing a known fifty-gram spice packet. Five readings in grams: forty-nine point eight, fifty point two, fifty point one, forty-nine point nine, fifty point zero. The average is fifty grams exactly. Sigma works out to about zero point one four grams. So the scale reads fifty point zero plus or minus zero point one four grams — a very tight, reliable scale! <<WRITE_TEXT:Repeat → average → sigma = honest uncertainty|id=text-2>>The pattern is always the same: repeat, average, find sigma. <<FOCUS:sigma-band>> So every time you report an experimental result, remember two things. First, random errors never vanish — your only weapon against them is repetition and averaging. Second, sigma is not a sign of failure. It is the honest, quantified statement of how confident you are in your answer. <<POINT:sigma-band>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> You measure the same lens ten times and get ten different answers — so which one do you write down? <<SECTION:Repeated Measurements & Uncertainty|id=sec-1>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:readings-column>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:25_7:deviation_table>> <<WRITE_TEXT:10 readings — all slightly different|id=text-1>>The ten readings in centimeters are: twenty-five point four, twenty-five point two, twenty-five point six, twenty-five point one, twenty-five point three, twenty-five point two, twenty-five point five, twenty-five point four, twenty-five point three, and twenty-five point seven. None of them are identical — and that is completely normal. We add up all ten readings and divide by ten — that gives us the best single estimate, the average. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\bar{f} = \frac{1}{10}\sum_{i=1}^{10} f_i = 25.37 \approx 25.4 \text{ cm}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:average-line>> <<WRITE_STEP:Average = sum of all 10 readings ÷ 10|id=step-1>>The honest answer starts with the average — add all ten values and divide by ten. That gives us twenty-five point three seven, which we round to twenty-five point four centimeters. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> <<FOCUS:deviation-column>> <<SECTION:Computing Standard Deviation σ|id=sec-2>>But twenty-five point four alone is not the full story. Some readings were as low as twenty-five point one and as high as twenty-five point seven — the average does not tell you about that scatter. That is where the standard deviation sigma comes in. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Deviation = fi − f-bar for each reading|id=step-2>>For each of the ten readings, we subtract the average. Reading one: twenty-five point four minus twenty-five point four equals zero. Reading four: twenty-five point one minus twenty-five point four equals minus zero point three. We fill in every row like this. <<TRACE:deviation-column>> <<POINT:deviation-column>> <<FOCUS:squared-deviation-column>> <<WRITE_STEP:Square each deviation|id=step-3>>Now we square every deviation. Negative signs disappear — minus zero point three squared becomes zero point zero nine. Zero squared stays zero. This is intentional: squaring stops positive and negative errors from cancelling each other out. <<TRACE:squared-deviation-column>> <<FOCUS:sum-row>> <<WRITE_STEP:Sum of squared deviations = 0.33 cm²|id=step-4>>Add all ten squared deviations together: zero point zero zero plus zero point zero four plus zero point zero four, all the way down — the total is zero point three three centimeters squared. Take each deviation, square it, average the squares, then take the square root — that is the standard deviation sigma. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{10}\sum_{i=1}^{10}(f_i - \bar{f})^2} = \sqrt{0.033} \approx 0.18 \approx 0.2 \text{ cm}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:sigma-result>> <<WRITE_STEP:σ = √(0.33 ÷ 10) = √0.033 ≈ 0.18 ≈ 0.2 cm|id=step-5>>Divide by ten to get zero point zero three three centimeters squared, then take the square root. The square root of zero point zero three three is approximately zero point one eight centimeters, which we round to zero point two centimeters. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:sigma-result>> <<WRITE_KEY:f = (25.4 ± 0.2) cm|id=key-1>>So we write the final result as f equals open bracket twenty-five point four plus or minus zero point two close bracket centimeters. The twenty-five point four is our best estimate; the zero point two is how much we honestly expect it to vary. <<PAUSE:short>> The final answer bundles the best estimate and the spread into one honest statement. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f = (25.4 \pm 0.2) \text{ cm}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Extended Example 1 — Reaction Time|id=sec-3>><<WRITE_TEXT:Reaction time: 5 trials (seconds)|id=text-2>>Let's try the same method with something more everyday. A student measures their reaction time five times in seconds and gets: zero point three one, zero point two eight, zero point three four, zero point three zero, and zero point two seven. <<WRITE_STEP:Average = (0.31+0.28+0.34+0.30+0.27) ÷ 5 = 0.30 s|id=step-6>>Adding those five values: zero point three one plus zero point two eight plus zero point three four plus zero point three zero plus zero point two seven equals one point five zero. Divide by five — the average reaction time is zero point three zero seconds. The squared deviations from zero point three zero are: zero point zero zero zero one, zero point zero zero zero four, zero point zero zero one six, zero point zero zero zero zero, and zero point zero zero zero nine. Their sum is zero point zero zero three zero seconds squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Σ(fi−f̄)² = 0.0030 s²|id=step-7>> <<WRITE_STEP:σ = √(0.0030 ÷ 5) = √0.00060 ≈ 0.024 ≈ 0.02 s|id=step-8>>Divide by five to get zero point zero zero zero six zero, and take the square root — sigma is approximately zero point zero two four seconds, rounded to zero point zero two seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Reaction time = (0.30 ± 0.02) s|id=ans-1>>So the reaction time is zero point three zero plus or minus zero point zero two seconds. Same method, different context — same honesty. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Extended Example 2 — Cooking Temperature|id=sec-4>><<WRITE_TEXT:Oven temp: 4 readings (°C)|id=text-3>>Now imagine a baker checks their oven temperature four times and records: one hundred ninety-eight, two hundred two, one hundred ninety-nine, and two hundred one degrees Celsius. She wants to know: is the oven reliably at two hundred degrees? <<PAUSE:long>> <<WRITE_STEP:Average = (198+202+199+201) ÷ 4 = 200 °C|id=step-9>>Average: one hundred ninety-eight plus two hundred two plus one hundred ninety-nine plus two hundred one equals eight hundred. Divide by four — the average is exactly two hundred degrees Celsius. <<PAUSE:short>> Deviations from two hundred: minus two, plus two, minus one, plus one. Squared: four, four, one, one. Sum equals ten degrees squared. Divide by four: two point five degrees squared. Square root: approximately one point six degrees. <<WRITE_STEP:σ = √(10 ÷ 4) = √2.5 ≈ 1.6 °C|id=step-10>><<WRITE_ANSWER:Oven temp = (200 ± 2) °C|id=ans-2>>Rounding to one significant figure, sigma is about two degrees, so the oven temperature is two hundred plus or minus two degrees Celsius — yes, it is reliably at two hundred! <<WRITE_KEY:Any measurement = best estimate ± spread|id=key-2>>Every time you repeat a measurement, the average is your best guess and the standard deviation is your honest admission of how much the readings scatter. A measurement without an uncertainty is an incomplete measurement — always write both. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<FOCUS:origin-O>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:5_0 m:vector_components_diagram>> What if three forces all the same size pull on a knot from different directions — can you find exactly where the knot moves, just by breaking each pull into two number lines? That is the whole game of vector components, and we are about to play it with three vectors at once. <<SECTION:Vector Components & Resultant|id=sec-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:vector-OC>> Here are our three vectors — OA, OB, and OC — all starting from origin O. All three vectors OA, OB, and OC have equal magnitude F. OA makes thirty degrees with the x-axis, OB makes sixty degrees, and OC makes one hundred thirty five degrees, pushing into the second quadrant. Notice that OC tilts past the y-axis, which is the detail that will flip its x-component negative. <<WRITE_TEXT:OA=OB=OC=F; angles 30°, 60°, 135°|id=text-1>> <<TRACE:vector-OC>> <<POINT:vector-OC>> <<FOCUS:angle-OC>> The combination we are computing is OA plus OB minus OC. Let us gather all three x-components first. The x-component of OA is F cosine thirty, which is F root three over two. The x-component of OB is F cosine sixty, which is F over two. The x-component of OC is F cosine one hundred thirty five, which is negative F over root two — negative, just as we expected. <<WRITE_STEP:x: F√3/2 + F/2 − (−F/√2)|id=step-1>> Now subtract OC's x-component from the sum. Subtracting a negative flips to addition: F root three over two plus F over two plus F over root two, which factors neatly to F over two times the quantity root three plus one plus root two. That is the total x-component of the resultant. <<WRITE_STEP:x-total = F/2 (√3 + 1 + √2)|id=step-2>> <<POINT:vector-OA>> The total x-component is the sum of all three x-projections, where subtracting OC flips its negative sign to positive. <<WRITE_EQUATION:R_x = F\cos 30^\circ + F\cos 60^\circ - F\cos 135^\circ = \frac{F}{2}(\sqrt{3}+1+\sqrt{2})|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:y-axis>> Now the y-components. The y-component of OA is F cosine sixty, which is F over two. The y-component of OB is F cosine one hundred fifty, which is negative F root three over two. The y-component of OC is F cosine forty five, which is F over root two. Combining them: F over two minus F root three over two minus F over root two equals F over two times the quantity one minus root three minus root two. <<WRITE_STEP:y-total = F/2 (1 − √3 − √2)|id=step-3>> The total y-component combines OA's positive contribution with OB's negative and OC's contribution, leaving a net downward component. <<WRITE_EQUATION:R_y = \frac{F}{2}(1 - \sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2})|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The angle of the resultant with the x-axis is the inverse tangent of the y-component divided by the x-component. The F over two cancels, leaving inverse tangent of the quantity one minus root three minus root two, all divided by one plus root three plus root two. That is our final answer for example one. <<WRITE_STEP:θ = tan⁻¹[(1−√3−√2)/(1+√3+√2)]|id=step-4>> <<PAUSE:short>> The angle of the resultant is found by dividing the y-component by the x-component and taking the inverse tangent. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2}}{1+\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}}\right)|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Example two uses a beautiful symmetry shortcut. Three vectors OA, OB, and OC all start from center O of a circle of radius R. OA equals OC in magnitude, both equal to R, and they are symmetric about OB, each making forty five degrees with OB. <<SECTION:Symmetric Vectors Shortcut|id=sec-2>> <<WRITE_TEXT:OA=OB=OC=R; OA & OC symmetric about OB|id=text-2>> When two vectors are mirror images about a third, their sum points exactly along that bisector. The magnitude of OA plus OC equals two R times cosine of forty five degrees, which is R times root two. Adding OB, which is also R and points the same direction, the final resultant magnitude is R root two plus R, which equals R times the quantity one plus root two. <<WRITE_STEP:R√2 + R = R(1+√2)|id=step-5>> Example three: the resultant of vector OA and vector OB is perpendicular to OA. Here is the key question — if the resultant must point along the y-axis, what must be true about its x-component? <<SECTION:Perpendicular Resultant|id=sec-3>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The x-component of the resultant must be exactly zero! Vector OA has magnitude four meters along the x-axis, so its x-component is four. Vector OB has magnitude six meters at angle theta, so its x-component is six cosine theta. Setting four plus six cosine theta equals zero gives cosine theta equals negative two thirds, so theta equals inverse cosine of negative two thirds. <<WRITE_STEP:4 + 6cosθ = 0 → cosθ = −2/3|id=step-6>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:θ = cos⁻¹(−2/3)|id=ans-1>> Because the resultant must point along the y-axis, its x-component must be zero, giving this equation for theta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:4 + 6\cos\theta = 0 \implies \cos\theta = -\tfrac{2}{3}|id=eq-4|boxed>> Example four: write the unit vector in the direction of A, where A has components five in the i direction, one in the j direction, and negative two in the k direction. The magnitude of A equals the square root of twenty five plus one plus four, which equals the square root of thirty. Dividing each component by the magnitude gives the unit vector: five over root thirty in i, one over root thirty in j, and negative two over root thirty in k. <<SECTION:Unit Vectors & Dot Products|id=sec-4>> <<WRITE_STEP:|A| = √(25+1+4) = √30|id=step-7>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Â = (5i + j − 2k)/√30|id=ans-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> Example five asks us to prove something surprising: if the magnitude of a plus b equals the magnitude of a minus b, what must be true about a and b? Squaring both magnitudes: magnitude squared of a plus b equals a squared plus b squared plus two times a dot b. Magnitude squared of a minus b equals a squared plus b squared minus two times a dot b. If the magnitudes are equal, the squared magnitudes are equal, so two times a dot b equals negative two times a dot b, forcing a dot b to equal zero. A dot product of zero means the vectors are perpendicular. <<WRITE_STEP:|a+b|²=a²+b²+2a·b; |a−b|²=a²+b²−2a·b|id=step-8>> <<WRITE_KEY:If |a+b|=|a−b|, then a⊥b|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> When the squared magnitudes of the sum and difference are set equal, all terms cancel except the dot product, which must be zero. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0 \implies \vec{a} \perp \vec{b}|id=eq-5|boxed>> Example six: find the angle between vector a equals two i plus three j plus four k, and vector b equals four i plus three j plus two k. The dot product a dot b equals two times four plus three times three plus four times two, which is eight plus nine plus eight, equals twenty five. The magnitude of a equals the square root of four plus nine plus sixteen equals the square root of twenty nine. The magnitude of b equals the square root of sixteen plus nine plus four, also the square root of twenty nine. So cosine theta equals twenty five over twenty nine, giving theta equals inverse cosine of twenty five over twenty nine. <<WRITE_STEP:a·b = 8+9+8 = 25; |a|=|b|=√29|id=step-9>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:θ = cos⁻¹(25/29)|id=ans-3>> Example seven computes the scalar triple product. Vector A equals two i plus three j plus seven k, vector B equals i plus two k, and vector C equals j plus k. First find B cross C: i cross j gives k, i cross k gives negative j, two k cross j gives negative two i, and two k cross k gives zero. So B cross C equals negative two i minus j plus k. Now dot that with A: two times negative two plus three times negative one plus seven times one equals negative four minus three plus seven equals zero. <<SECTION:Triple Product & Calculus|id=sec-5>> <<WRITE_STEP:B×C = −2i − j + k|id=step-10>> <<WRITE_STEP:A·(B×C) = −4−3+7 = 0|id=step-11>> Now calculus. The volume of a sphere is four thirds times pi times R cubed. Differentiating with respect to R: d V over d R equals four thirds times pi times three R squared, which simplifies to four pi R squared — that is just the surface area of the sphere! When the radius changes from twenty point zero centimeters to twenty point one centimeters, delta R equals zero point one centimeters. At R equals twenty centimeters, the rate equals four pi times four hundred equals one thousand six hundred pi square centimeters. The change in volume is one thousand six hundred pi times zero point one equals one hundred sixty pi cubic centimeters. <<WRITE_STEP:dV/dR = 4πR²|id=step-12>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:ΔV = 160π cm³|id=ans-4>> Differentiating the volume formula gives the surface area, and multiplying by the small change in radius gives the volume change. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{dV}{dR} = 4\pi R^2, \quad \Delta V = 160\pi \text{ cm}^3|id=eq-6|boxed>> Three differentiation rules in one example. For y equals x squared times sine x, the product rule gives x squared times cosine x plus sine x times two x, which simplifies to x times the quantity two sine x plus x cosine x. For y equals sine x divided by x, the quotient rule gives x cosine x minus sine x, all divided by x squared. For y equals sine of x squared, the chain rule gives cosine of x squared times two x. <<WRITE_STEP:Product: d/dx(x²sinx) = x(2sinx + xcosx)|id=step-13>> <<WRITE_STEP:Quotient: d/dx(sinx/x) = (xcosx−sinx)/x²|id=step-14>> <<WRITE_STEP:Chain: d/dx(sin(x²)) = 2xcos(x²)|id=step-15>> Finding a minimum: y equals x plus one over x for x greater than zero. The derivative is one minus one over x squared. Setting that to zero: x equals one or x equals negative one, but only x equals one is valid here. At x equals one, y equals one plus one equals two. Near x equals zero, y blows up because of the one over x term. For very large x, y blows up because of the x term. So x equals one is a minimum, and the minimum value is two. <<WRITE_STEP:dy/dx = 1 − 1/x² = 0 → x = 1|id=step-16>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:min y = 2 at x = 1|id=ans-5>> <<FOCUS:curve-y-x-squared>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:5_0 m:parabola_area_diagram>> Integration as area. The curve is y equals x squared. <<SECTION:Integration|id=sec-6>> <<FOCUS:strip-dx>> We divide the region under the curve into thin vertical strips between x equals zero and x equals six. Each strip has height x squared and width dx, so its tiny area is d A equals x squared d x. <<TRACE:strip-dx>> <<FOCUS:shaded-region>> Adding all those strips from x equals zero to x equals six means integrating x squared d x between those limits. The antiderivative is x cubed over three. Evaluating: six cubed over three minus zero is two hundred sixteen over three, which equals seventy two square units. <<WRITE_STEP:∫₀⁶ x² dx = [x³/3]₀⁶ = 216/3 = 72|id=step-17>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Area = 72 square units|id=ans-6>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Example eleven integrates A times sine of omega t from zero to t, where A and omega are constants. The antiderivative of sine of omega t is negative cosine of omega t divided by omega. Evaluating at the limits: A over omega times the quantity one minus cosine of omega t. <<WRITE_STEP:∫₀ᵗ A sin(ωt)dt = (A/ω)(1 − cosωt)|id=step-18>> Example twelve separates variables. The relation is v times d v over d x equals negative omega squared times x. Rearranging: v d v equals negative omega squared x d x. Integrating left side from v naught to v and right side from zero to x: one half v squared minus one half v naught squared equals negative omega squared x squared over two. Solving: v equals the square root of the quantity v naught squared minus omega squared x squared. <<WRITE_STEP:∫v dv = −ω²∫x dx → v²= v₀²−ω²x²|id=step-19>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:v = √(v₀² − ω²x²)|id=ans-7>> After separating variables and integrating both sides with their respective limits, we solve for v to get velocity as a function of displacement. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v = \sqrt{v_0^2 - \omega^2 x^2}|id=eq-7|boxed>> Example thirteen: the charge element d q equals e to the negative t over tau times d t. Integrating from t equals zero to t equals tau, the antiderivative of e to the negative t over tau is negative tau times e to the negative t over tau. Evaluating at the limits gives tau times the quantity one minus one over e. <<WRITE_STEP:Q = ∫₀^τ e^(−t/τ)dt = τ(1 − 1/e)|id=step-20>> Example fourteen — significant figures. Adding twenty one point six zero zero two, two hundred thirty four, two thousand seven hundred thirty two point one zero, and thirteen: the least precise column is the ones place, so we round to twenty two, two hundred thirty four, two thousand seven hundred thirty two, and thirteen. Their sum is two thousand nine hundred eighty eight. Multiplying by thirteen, which has only two significant digits, gives thirty eight thousand eight hundred forty four, which rounds to thirty nine thousand. <<SECTION:Significant Figures|id=sec-7>> <<WRITE_STEP:Round to ones: 22+234+2732+13 = 2988|id=step-21>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:2988 × 13 ≈ 39000 (2 sig. figs.)|id=ans-8>> Extended example one — cooking. A recipe uses three ingredient forces on a balance: vector P of magnitude five newtons at zero degrees, vector Q of magnitude five newtons at ninety degrees, and vector R of magnitude five newtons at one hundred eighty degrees. Break into components: P has x equals five, Q has x equals zero, R has x equals negative five. Total x equals zero. P has y equals zero, Q has y equals five, R has y equals zero. Total y equals five. The resultant has magnitude five newtons pointing straight up along the y-axis, at ninety degrees. <<SECTION:Extended Examples|id=sec-8>> <<WRITE_STEP:P+Q+R: x=5+0−5=0, y=0+5+0=5|id=step-22>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Resultant = 5 N at 90°|id=ans-9>> Extended example two — a delivery bike. A courier's position vector is A equals three i plus four j kilometers, and a second delivery point is B equals six i plus zero j kilometers. Find the angle between routes OA and OB. Dot product A dot B equals three times six plus four times zero equals eighteen. Magnitude of A is the square root of nine plus sixteen equals five. Magnitude of B is six. Cosine theta equals eighteen over thirty, which equals three over five, so theta equals inverse cosine of zero point six, approximately fifty three point one degrees. <<WRITE_STEP:A·B=18; |A|=5, |B|=6 → cosθ=18/30=3/5|id=step-23>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:θ = cos⁻¹(3/5) ≈ 53.1°|id=ans-10>> Extended example three — a savings account. The total savings S in thousands of rupees follows S equals t squared plus one over t for t between one and three years. The rate of change of savings with time is d S over d t equals two t minus one over t squared. At t equals one year, the rate is two minus one equals one thousand rupees per year. The minimum savings occurs where two t minus one over t squared equals zero, giving two t cubed equals one, so t equals the cube root of one half. For t greater than one, savings only grows — the minimum in that range is at t equals one, where S equals one plus one equals two thousand rupees. <<WRITE_STEP:dS/dt = 2t − 1/t² = 0 → t = (1/2)^(1/3)|id=step-24>> <<WRITE_KEY:Resolve vectors into components; combine separately|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> What if adding a bunch of messy decimal numbers gave you a perfectly clean answer — would you trust it? And what if it didn't — would you know how many digits to keep? That judgment call is exactly what significant digits in addition is all about. <<FOCUS:addend-list>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:physics_and_mathematics:280_7:addition_breakdown>> <<SECTION:Adding with significant digits|id=sec-1>>Let's set the scene. Suppose a physicist measures four lengths and writes them down: one hundred eight point three, ninety-six point four, forty-seven point eight five, and twenty-eight point one five. <<TRACE:addend-list>> <<FOCUS:decimal-marker>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Least decimal places = limit|id=text-1>>Before we even add, here is the key rule: the answer can only be as precise as the least precise number in the list. Look at the addends — some go to two decimal places, but some only go to one. That one-decimal-place number sets the ceiling. <<POINT:decimal-marker>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:raw-sum-label>> Here is the honest question: if we just punch all four numbers into a calculator, we get two hundred eighty point seven zero — two decimal places. Should we write down both of those decimal places in our final answer? <<PAUSE:long>> The raw calculator total is two hundred eighty point seven zero, but we round to one decimal place because that is the precision our least precise measurement allows. <<WRITE_EQUATION:108.3 + 96.4 + 47.85 + 28.15 = 280.70 \approx 280.7|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rounded-sum-label>> <<WRITE_STEP:Round to fewest d.p. → 1 d.p.|id=step-1>>No — because our least precise measurement only gave us one decimal place. Keeping the second decimal would be a lie about how well we actually measured. So we round to one decimal place, and the answer becomes two hundred eighty point seven. <<TRACE:rounded-sum-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rounded-sum-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:Sum = 280.7 (1 d.p.)|id=key-1>>The sum is two hundred eighty point seven. Not two eighty point seven zero, not two eighty point seven something — exactly two hundred eighty point seven, rounded to one decimal place because that is all our data supports. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Precision limited by weakest input|id=text-2>>Think of it like a chain: the whole chain is only as strong as its weakest link. Your sum is only as precise as your least precise addend. Adding more decimal places to your answer does not give you more precision — it gives you false confidence. <<POINT:decimal-marker>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:sum-line>> <<WRITE_KEY:In addition: match fewest decimal places|id=key-2>>So here is the takeaway you carry into every physics calculation: when you add, count the decimal places in each number, find the fewest, and that is exactly how many decimal places your answer gets. That is why the sum is two hundred eighty point seven — and that answer is both correct and honest. <<TRACE:sum-line>> <<PAUSE:short>>

lesson_plans.title: Vectors and Scalars

hook.text: If I tell you a car is moving at sixty kilometers per hour — do you actually know where it's going?

crucial_facts: A scalar is fully described by a number and a unit alone; a vector needs both a magnitude AND a direction.
A vector is drawn as an arrow — its length represents magnitude, and the arrowhead points in the direction of the quantity.

diagrams.purpose: Show how vectors are drawn as arrows with tail, head, and proportional length — using several velocity examples at different magnitudes and directions.

required_elements.description: A short arrow representing a small velocity, labeled '2 m/s', showing tail and head.
A medium arrow representing a velocity of 4 m/s in a different direction.
A longer arrow representing a velocity of 6 m/s in yet another direction, demonstrating that length is proportional to magnitude.
A label marking the tail (rear end) of one of the arrows.
A label marking the head (front end, with arrowhead) of one of the arrows.
A small bracket or bar beneath the arrows indicating the unit length that represents one meter per second.

choreography.narration: If I tell you a car is moving at sixty kilometers per hour — do you actually know where it's going? No! You know HOW FAST, but not WHICH WAY. That gap between those two ideas is what this lesson is all about.

<<SECTION:Scalars — number and unit only|id=sec-1>>Some quantities in physics are perfectly happy with just a number and a unit. <<WRITE_TEXT:Scalar = number + unit|id=text-1>>Take mass. If I say an object has a mass of five kilograms, you know everything there is to know. There is no 'which direction is the mass?' — it simply has none.

<<WRITE_TEXT:e.g. mass: 5 kg + 2 kg = 7 kg|id=text-2>>If you combine a five kilogram object with a two kilogram object, the total is just seven kilograms. Ordinary addition — no tricks. That's the beauty of scalars: they obey everyday arithmetic.

<<SECTION:Vectors — magnitude AND direction|id=sec-2>>But now back to that car. Speed alone isn't enough. <<WRITE_TEXT:Vector = magnitude + direction|id=text-3>>Quantities that need BOTH a size and a direction — those are called vectors. Velocity is the classic example: five meters per second NORTH is completely different from five meters per second EAST.
So how do we draw a vector? We draw it as an arrow. Let's build that picture now.

Here is our first velocity arrow — small, representing two meters per second. <<WRITE_TEXT:Length ∝ magnitude|id=text-4>>The length of the arrow is proportional to the magnitude. First, we agree on a unit length — say, one centimeter for every one meter per second.
The back end of the arrow — where it starts — is called the tail. The front end, where the arrowhead sits, is called the head. The head always points in the direction of the quantity.

Now here is a second arrow for a velocity of four meters per second — pointing in a different direction. Notice it is twice as long as the two meters per second arrow. And here is a third one: six meters per second, even longer. <<WRITE_TEXT:Head = direction; tail = origin|id=text-5>>The direction each arrow POINTS is the direction of the velocity.

<<WRITE_KEY:Vector = arrow: length is magnitude, direction is the arrowhead|id=key-1>>So the whole idea crystallizes into one picture: a vector IS an arrow. Its length tells you how big. Its tip tells you which way. That's it.

Here's a question worth thinking about: if I give a ball two velocities at the same time — say, three meters per second to the right AND four meters per second upward — what is its actual velocity? Is it just three plus four equals seven meters per second?

The answer is no — and that's the deep reason vectors exist as a special category. You cannot just add the numbers. The actual speed turns out to be five meters per second — at an angle — because directions matter. Vectors add geometrically, not numerically. We will explore exactly HOW in the next topic.

<<WRITE_KEY:Scalars add normally; vectors add geometrically|id=key-2>>So here is the big takeaway: scalars like mass and temperature obey ordinary arithmetic. Vectors like velocity and force obey their own rules — because direction is baked in. <<WRITE_TEXT:Examples — scalars: mass, temp, speed. Vectors: velocity, force, displacement|id=text-6>>Whenever you meet a new quantity in physics, ask yourself: does it have a direction? If yes, it's a vector.

equations.explanation_in_words: We write a vector with an arrow on top of the symbol — it's our shorthand for saying this quantity has both a size and a direction.

lesson_plans.title: Equality of Vectors

hook.text: Imagine two cars, both doing sixty kilometers per hour. Are their velocity vectors equal? Most people say yes — but they might be completely wrong.

crucial_facts: Two vectors are equal only if BOTH their magnitude AND their direction are the same.
Parallel translation of a vector — sliding it to a new position — does NOT change it; position on the page is irrelevant to equality.

diagrams.purpose: Show one equal pair (same length, same direction, different positions) and one unequal pair (same length, different directions) to make both conditions for equality vivid.

required_elements.description: First vector of the equal pair: a rightward arrow of length 3 units, positioned on the left side of the diagram.
Second vector of the equal pair: a rightward arrow of the same length 3 units, positioned lower and to the right of equal-vec-a, parallel to it.
First vector of the unequal pair: a rightward arrow of length 3 units, positioned on the right side of the diagram.
Second vector of the unequal pair: an upward arrow of the same length 3 units, positioned near unequal-vec-a, clearly pointing a different direction.
Label reading 'EQUAL' between equal-vec-a and equal-vec-b.
Label reading 'NOT EQUAL' between unequal-vec-a and unequal-vec-b.

choreography.narration: Imagine two cars, both doing sixty kilometers per hour. Are their velocity vectors equal? Most people say yes — but they might be completely wrong.

<<SECTION:What makes two vectors equal?|id=sec-1>>A vector carries two pieces of information: its magnitude — how big it is — and its direction — which way it points. So to decide if two vectors are equal, you must check BOTH.

<<WRITE_KEY:Equal vectors: same magnitude AND same direction|id=key-1>>Both conditions must be satisfied — not just one. Same magnitude but different direction? Not equal. Same direction but different magnitude? Also not equal.

Back to those two cars. One heads north at sixty kilometers per hour, the other heads east at sixty kilometers per hour. Same speed — same magnitude. But the directions are different. So are their velocity vectors equal?
No — they are NOT equal. Look at the unequal pair here: same arrow length, but one points right and one points up. Different direction means different vector, full stop.

<<SECTION:Parallel translation|id=sec-2>>Now look at the equal pair. These two arrows are nowhere near each other on the board — they sit in completely different positions. Yet they are perfectly equal. Why?
Because a vector does NOT care where it lives on the page. If you slide — or parallel-translate — a vector to a new spot without rotating it or stretching it, it is still the exact same vector.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Parallel translation → vector unchanged|id=text-1>>Think of it like a compass bearing. North is north — it doesn't matter whether you draw the north arrow in London or in Tokyo. The direction is the same, so if the lengths match too, the vectors are equal.
So the checklist is simple: step one — magnitudes equal? Step two — directions equal? If both answers are yes, the vectors are equal, no matter where on the board you drew them.

<<WRITE_KEY:Position on page is irrelevant to vector equality|id=key-2>>Remember: two conditions, both required — same magnitude, same direction. That is the complete definition of equality for vectors.

lesson_plans.title: Addition of Vectors

hook.text: Walk five metres north, then five metres east — you haven't gone ten metres from where you started. So what does 'five plus five' actually mean for vectors?

crucial_facts: The sum of two vectors is found by placing them tip-to-tail — the resultant is the arrow from the very first tail to the very last head.
When the angle between two vectors of magnitudes a and b is theta, the magnitude of their sum is the square root of a squared plus b squared plus two a b cosine theta.

diagrams.purpose: Show the triangle rule (tip-to-tail) and the parallelogram rule as two views of the same vector sum, then expose the geometry used to derive the magnitude formula.

required_elements.description: Vector a drawn as a bold arrow from point A to point B, labelled 'a' at its midpoint.
Vector b drawn tip-to-tail after a, starting at point B (head of a) and ending at point D, labelled 'b'.
The resultant vector drawn from A (tail of a) to D (head of b), labelled 'a+b' in a distinct colour.
A copy of vector b starting from A (same tail as a), used to complete the parallelogram, labelled 'b'.
The full parallelogram with vertices A, B, D, C formed by vectors a and b from the common tail A.
The diagonal of the parallelogram from A to D, highlighted in a distinct colour to represent the resultant, labelled 'a+b'.
Arc and label theta at vertex A showing the angle between vectors a and b.
A dashed perpendicular dropped from D to the extension of AB, meeting at point E, labelled to show b sin theta (vertical) and b cos theta (horizontal projection).
Label 'b cos theta' along the horizontal segment from B to E.
Label 'b sin theta' along the vertical segment from E to D.

choreography.narration: Walk five metres north, then five metres east — you haven't gone ten metres from where you started. So what does 'five plus five' actually mean for vectors? Scalars just add up. Vectors carry direction, and that changes everything. <<SECTION:Adding Vectors|id=sec-1>>

<<WRITE_TEXT:Vectors carry magnitude AND direction|id=text-1>>Here is the key move. When you add vectors, you must respect both their size and the way they point. The trick is to chain them — place the tail of the second vector right at the head of the first.
So here is vector a, going from A to B. Now we place the tail of vector b exactly at B — the head of a — and let b go wherever it points, ending at D.

<<WRITE_KEY:Resultant = arrow from first tail to last head|id=key-1>>The resultant — the vector sum — is the single arrow that goes from A, where a started, all the way to D, where b ended. That one arrow does the job of both. This is the triangle rule.

Now here is a question worth sitting with for a second. The triangle rule says put them tip-to-tail. But what if both vectors happen to start at the same point — like two forces acting on one object from the same spot? How do you find the sum then?

<<WRITE_TEXT:Parallelogram rule — same tail, diagonal = sum|id=text-2>>Watch. Draw both a and b from the same tail at A. Now complete the parallelogram — slide copies of each vector to make the four sides. The diagonal shooting out from A to the far corner D is exactly the same resultant. Two rules, one answer.
Both the triangle rule and the parallelogram rule lead to exactly the same diagonal AD. They are two faces of the same idea — pick whichever one is easier to draw in a given situation.

<<SECTION:Finding the magnitude|id=sec-2>>Good. Now let's figure out how long that resultant arrow actually is. The angle between a and b is theta. Let's drop a perpendicular from D down to the line AB extended — meeting it at E.

That perpendicular chops the picture into a neat right triangle AED. The horizontal leg AE has length a plus b cosine theta, and the vertical leg DE has length b sine theta. <<WRITE_STEP:AE = a + b cosθ, DE = b sinθ|id=step-1>>

Pythagoras on triangle AED gives AD squared equals AE squared plus DE squared — that is, open bracket a plus b cosine theta close bracket squared, plus open bracket b sine theta close bracket squared. Expand and use the identity sine squared plus cosine squared equals one, and you're left with a squared plus b squared plus two a b cosine theta. <<WRITE_STEP:AD² = (a + b cosθ)² + (b sinθ)²|id=step-2>> <<WRITE_STEP:= a² + b² + 2ab cosθ|id=step-3>>

<<WRITE_EQUATION:\|\vec{a}+\vec{b}\| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + 2ab\cos\theta}|id=eq-1>>So the magnitude of the resultant is the square root of a squared plus b squared plus two a b cosine theta. That formula lives inside the picture — it's just Pythagoras wearing a disguise.

And the direction? The resultant makes an angle alpha with a, where tangent of alpha equals b sine theta divided by a plus b cosine theta — again, straight from the same right triangle. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tan\alpha = \frac{b\sin\theta}{a + b\cos\theta}|id=eq-2>>

<<WRITE_KEY:Tip-to-tail → resultant from first tail to last head|id=key-2>>So here's the whole picture: place vectors tip-to-tail — or draw them from a shared tail and complete the parallelogram — and the arrow from start to finish is your answer. Its length comes from one clean formula, and its angle from simple trigonometry. The geometry does all the work.

equations.explanation_in_words: Pythagoras on the right triangle inside the parallelogram gives us the length of the diagonal — that's the magnitude of the resultant.
The angle the resultant makes with a comes straight from the same right triangle — opposite over adjacent.

lesson_plans.title: Multiplication of a Vector by a Number

hook.text: If I told you to walk five steps forward, you'd know exactly what to do. But what if I said: now do negative two of that? What does a negative number of steps even mean?

crucial_facts: Multiplying a vector by a positive number stretches or shrinks it but keeps its direction the same.
Multiplying a vector by a negative number reverses the direction of the vector.

diagrams.purpose: Show visually how a vector stretches, shrinks, and flips when multiplied by positive and negative scalars.

required_elements.description: A horizontal arrow pointing right, labeled 'a', of medium length, drawn in neutral color.
A horizontal arrow pointing right, labeled '2a', twice the length of vector-a, drawn below it in blue.
A horizontal arrow pointing right, labeled '½a', half the length of vector-a, drawn below 2a in green.
A horizontal arrow pointing LEFT, labeled '−a', same length as vector-a, drawn below half-a in red.
A horizontal arrow pointing LEFT, labeled '−2a', twice the length of vector-a, drawn below neg-a in red.
A short horizontal arrow pointing right, labeled 'û', length of one unit, drawn separately at the bottom with a bracket showing magnitude 1.

choreography.narration: If I told you to walk five steps forward, you'd know exactly what to do. But what if I said: now do negative two of that? What does a negative number of steps even mean? That's exactly what scalar multiplication of a vector answers.

<<SECTION:Scalar × Vector|id=sec-1>>Here's our starting point. <<WRITE_TEXT:Vector a — has magnitude and direction|id=text-1>>A vector called a is just an arrow — it has a size, called its magnitude, and it points somewhere. Let's say it points to the right.
Now multiply by two. The new vector is two a. Watch what happens — same direction, but the arrow is now twice as long.
Multiply by one half instead. The arrow shrinks — but it still points right. The direction hasn't changed at all, only the size has.

<<WRITE_KEY:Positive scalar → same direction, different size|id=key-1>>So here's the first rule to lock in: multiplying a vector by any positive number keeps the direction exactly the same — it only stretches or squashes the magnitude.

Now for the interesting part. What happens when the number is negative? Here's my question: if multiplying by two doubles the length in the forward direction, what should multiplying by negative two do?
It flips the arrow. Negative a points in the exact opposite direction — to the left — with the same length. Negative two a flips AND doubles. The negative sign is a direction-reverser.

<<WRITE_KEY:Negative scalar → reverses direction|id=key-2>>So the second rule: multiplying by a negative number always reverses the direction. The special case is multiplying by negative one — that simply inverts the vector without changing its size at all.

<<SECTION:Unit vector|id=sec-2>>There's a beautiful idea hiding here. Every vector can be split into two pieces: its size, and a pure direction. We give that pure direction its own name — the unit vector, written as u with a little hat. Its magnitude is exactly one.

<<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{a} = a\hat{u}|id=eq-1>>So any vector a equals its magnitude a, which is just a plain number, multiplied by the unit vector u-hat pointing in its direction. The number carries the size; the unit vector carries the direction. That's scalar multiplication doing the heavy lifting.

Let's zoom out. When you multiply a vector by a scalar k, the new magnitude is the absolute value of k times the original magnitude. Positive k — arrow stretches or shrinks, keeps pointing the same way. Negative k — arrow flips to the opposite direction, and its size scales by how big k is.

Think about what this means for physics. If velocity is a vector pointing north at ten meters per second, then negative one times that velocity is ten meters per second pointing south. The negative sign didn't change the speed — it changed the direction. That's the power of scalar multiplication.

equations.explanation_in_words: The magnitude of the new vector is just the absolute value of k multiplied by the original magnitude — the sign of k only decides the direction, not the size.
Any vector equals its magnitude — a plain number — times a unit vector pointing in its direction.

lesson_plans.title: Subtraction of Vectors

hook.text: Here's a strange question — what if I told you that subtraction doesn't actually exist in the world of vectors? That every subtraction is secretly just an addition?

crucial_facts: Vector subtraction A minus B is the same as adding A and negative B, where negative B is B flipped by one hundred and eighty degrees.
The magnitude of A minus B is found using the cosine rule with the angle between A and negative B.

diagrams.purpose: Show side-by-side construction of A plus B and A minus B using the tip-to-tail method, with negative B clearly shown as the flipped version of B.

required_elements.description: Vector A drawn as a bold arrow pointing to the upper right.
Vector B drawn as a bold arrow pointing to the right, starting from the same origin as A.
Negative B drawn as a dashed bold arrow pointing to the left, the exact reverse of B, placed tip-to-tail after A.
Resultant arrow from the tail of A to the tip of B in the A plus B construction, labeled 'A+B'.
Resultant arrow from the tail of A to the tip of negative B in the A minus B construction, labeled 'A−B'.
Arc and label showing the angle theta between vector A and vector B at their common origin.
Arc and label showing the angle between vector A and vector negative B, which is one hundred and eighty degrees minus theta.

choreography.narration: Here's a strange question — what if I told you that subtraction doesn't actually exist in the world of vectors? That every subtraction is secretly just an addition?

<<SECTION:Vector Subtraction = Addition in Disguise|id=sec-1>>You already know that to add two vectors, you place them tip to tail and draw the resultant. Now watch what happens when we ask: what is A minus B?
Here is vector A, and here is vector B. If B points to the right, what do you think negative B looks like?

<<WRITE_TEXT:Negative B = B flipped 180°|id=text-1>>Exactly — negative B is just B rotated by one hundred and eighty degrees. Same length, opposite direction. That's all multiplication by negative one does to a vector.
<<WRITE_KEY:A − B = A + (−B)|id=key-1>>So A minus B is defined as: take A, then add negative B. Subtraction IS addition — you just flip one of the vectors first.
Let's build it on the diagram. We place negative B tip to tail after A — just like we always do when adding vectors.
The resultant drawn from the tail of A to the tip of negative B — that arrow right there — is A minus B.
Compare that to A plus B on the same diagram. Notice how the two resultants point in very different directions — the only thing that changed was the direction of one vector.
Now here is the key question for finding the magnitude: if the angle between A and B is theta, what is the angle between A and negative B?

<<WRITE_STEP:angle between A and −B = 180° − θ|id=step-1>>Because negative B is flipped, the angle opens up to one hundred and eighty degrees minus theta. If A and B were sixty degrees apart, then A and negative B are one hundred and twenty degrees apart.

<<WRITE_STEP:|A−B|² = |A|² + |B|² − 2|A||B|cos θ|id=step-2>>And once you have that angle, you find the magnitude using the same cosine rule you used for vector addition — just with that new angle plugged in.

<<WRITE_KEY:Subtraction = flip B, then add tip-to-tail|id=key-2>>So remember: there is no separate rule for subtraction. Flip the vector, add it tip to tail, apply the cosine rule. Subtraction is addition in disguise — every single time.

equations.explanation_in_words: A minus B means we add A to negative B — flip B by one hundred and eighty degrees and then add it tip to tail.
The magnitude of A minus B is found with the cosine rule, using the angle between A and negative B, which is one hundred and eighty degrees minus theta.

lesson_plans.title: Resolution of Vectors

hook.text: What if I told you that every single vector — no matter how weirdly it's pointing — is secretly just two ordinary arrows in disguise, one going sideways and one going straight up?

crucial_facts: A vector in the X-Y plane can be broken into two components: a cosine of alpha along the X-axis and a cosine of beta along the Y-axis, where alpha and beta are the angles it makes with those axes.
The components of a vector are its projections onto the coordinate axes — the 'shadows' it casts — and together they completely rebuild the original vector.
